‘The Shipping Industry’s False Solution: LNG and the Myth of Clean Shipping’ - indicates that the shipping industry is one of the biggest contributors to global greenhouse gas emissions. It is estimated that if nothing is done to change the current situation, the shipping industry will be responsible for 17% of global greenhouse gas emissions by 2050.

The Government has done little to address this issue. In fact, it has done very little to address any aspect of emissions from ships. The only action taken is to increase the cost of emissions to the Irish taxpayer by introducing a carbon tax.

The Minister for Communications, Climate Action and Environment has admitted that the carbon tax is an inadequate instrument in dealing with the issue of greenhouse gas emissions.

The Government does not seem to understand that the carbon tax is not an appropriate response to the issue. If the Government truly wants to tackle the issue of greenhouse gas emissions, it should take real action on reducing emissions from the shipping industry. The Government should engage in diplomacy with other countries and the European Union to achieve this end. It should also implement policy that encourages the use of alternative technologies and fuels.

In summary, the Government's approach to greenhouse gas emissions is inadequate and lacks ambition. The Government must take real action to address this global issue. This includes engaging in diplomacy with other countries and the European Union to reduce emissions from the shipping industry, and implementing policy that encourages the use of alternative technologies and fuels. The Government's current approach of imposing a carbon tax on Irish taxpayers is not a solution to the problem and is likely to have a negligible impact on overall emissions.

The hon. Gentleman is absolutely right: the Bill is about people in the armed forces who have a criminal conviction. I am not sure what his point was about the CPS. The CPS is not involved in the Bill; the Bill is about people who have a criminal conviction and are still serving in the armed forces. Let me turn to the question of the number of people affected. The Government estimate that there will be around 200 people affected by the Bill’s provisions. nothing has changed. How do you describe this as a breakthrough, and what would you say to the farmers and the people who voted for you because you promised a solution to this?

There are two parts to this question. The first part is: what is the breakthrough? The breakthrough is this. When we took office in 2015, we inherited a relationship with India that had been frozen for 20 years. For 20 years, there was no movement. We had a very strong position, which was to have a zero-tolerance policy for any product coming into this country that was fumigated, because of our own domestic and international obligations. We had to protect the industry and the environment. We had no flexibility whatsoever. So, if India wanted to sell us products, they had to find a way to do it without using fumigants.

The previous government had tried to negotiate this issue, but it didn't get anywhere. So, when we came into office, we inherited a very difficult situation. We spent a lot of time negotiating with the Indian government, and we have made significant progress. India has changed its practices and is no longer fumigating products that come into the Caribbean. So, that is the breakthrough.

The second part of your question is: what do I say to the farmers who have been suffering for a long time? I would say this: we have made significant progress, and we will continue to work on this issue until it is resolved. It is not just about the fumigation issue; it is also about other trade issues, such as the high cost of transportation, the lack of access to markets, and the lack of a level playing field for our farmers. We are working on all of these issues, and we will continue to fight for our farmers and for the people of this country.

During a visit to the Mid West this month I saw first hand the impact the housing crisis is having on people in my constituency. I met with a local community group who have been forced to set up a homeless charity. In the last two months alone they have had to assist 17 families, many of whom were homeless because of the Government's inaction on housing. In one case a family were placed in temporary accommodation in a local hotel. Another family were homeless for three months because they were waiting for a local authority to provide them with accommodation. A young woman was left with no alternative but to sleep in her car with her children.

The report showed a 58% increase in the number of families with children experiencing homelessness. I have written to the Taoiseach on behalf of these families, who have been failed by this Government, and I have asked him to take urgent action to address the crisis. He needs to provide additional funding to tackle the shortage of social and affordable housing, increase the number of rent supplement places and establish a task force to deal with the crisis in homelessness.

This report confirms that the Government's housing policies have failed. The Taoiseach must now act to ensure that families and individuals are not left to suffer because of his Government's inaction.

This is a very long time ago and the original purpose of the section needs to be reconsidered in the light of our modern understanding of child abuse.

The HSE’s recent decision to implement new standards for the minimum number of staff required to operate a home for the elderly is another example of the HSE’s lack of transparency. The HSE is proposing new standards for the minimum number of staff required to operate a home for the elderly. The new standards are as follows:

1. A minimum of 0.63 staff per resident during the day, with a minimum of 0.45 staff per resident during the night.
2. A minimum of 0.63 staff per resident at all times when the home is open.
3. A minimum of 0.63 staff per resident when the home is closed, but with the provision for a care worker to be on call.
4. A minimum of 0.63 staff per resident when the home is closed and the care worker is not on call.

These new standards are significantly lower than the current standards of 0.9 staff per resident during the day and 0.7 staff per resident during the night. The HSE claims that these new standards will bring Ireland in line with international best practice. However, the HSE has failed to provide any evidence to support this claim. The HSE has also failed to explain why these new standards are necessary.

The new standards are likely to result in the closure of many homes for the elderly. The HSE has admitted that up to 200 homes for the elderly may be forced to close as a result of these new standards. This is a devastating blow to the elderly and their families, who will be forced to find alternative care arrangements. The FOI Act 1997 introduced a new right of access to records held by public bodies, which has significantly contributed to transparency, accountability, and good governance. I acknowledge the importance of FOI in the functioning of our democracy and the role it plays in enhancing public trust in the activities of public bodies. The Act has provided citizens with the right to seek information from public bodies in a wide range of areas.

Since its introduction, the Act has been updated on three occasions, most recently in 2014, when the FOI Act 2014 was enacted. The Act has been instrumental in bringing about greater openness in our public bodies, but it is important to remember that it is only one of several key transparency mechanisms. The Act complements other transparency measures, such as the public sector register of interests, the mandatory disclosures regime, the Public Service Management Act 1997, the Whistleblower Act 2013, the Standards in Public Office Act 2001 and 2014 and the various provisions in the Companies Act 2014, among others.

The FOI Act 1997 has provided a framework for the release of information and has contributed to greater transparency and accountability. It has also created obligations on public bodies to document their activities and decisions, and to keep records. This has enabled the public to have a greater understanding of the work of public bodies.

The number of homeless people in Ireland has reached an all-time high. There were 10,645 homeless people in Ireland at the end of 2019, up 14% on the previous year. This is the highest number since homeless figures were first recorded in 2005. The Government’s response to this crisis has been inadequate. In fact, it has been woefully inadequate. The Government’s response has been to increase funding to local authorities to provide emergency accommodation, but it has not addressed the root causes of homelessness. It has not provided any real, meaningful solution to this crisis, but it is putting more money into the same failed system.

The Government has also failed to ensure that renters have the security they need, including through the introduction of long-term leases and rent certainty. Instead, it is planning to introduce a bill to change the law to make it easier for landlords to evict tenants who are in arrears of rent due to the COVID-19 pandemic. This is a short-term solution that will cause long-term problems. It will result in more people becoming homeless and it will result in more people living in poverty.

The Government needs to take a more holistic approach to addressing the root causes of homelessness. It needs to invest in affordable housing and it needs to ensure that renters have the security they need. It needs to address the underlying issues that are causing people to become homeless, such as high rents, a lack of affordable housing, and a lack of social welfare supports. It needs to take a proactive approach to preventing homelessness, rather than simply reacting to it.

In addition, the Government needs to ensure that there is adequate support for people who are already homeless

However, there is a bigger issue that the Committee, and indeed the whole House, needs to grapple with: we are moving towards a surveillance society that does not make us any safer. We cannot have it both ways. We cannot demand that we be protected from horrendous material and then say that we must not be watched, as though we can be free from terrorism and crime.

That is a choice that we must make, and it is a choice that we must make clearly and honestly. The more we demand to be protected from the horrible things that are done on the internet and on social media, the more we will be subject to surveillance and the more our freedoms will be eroded. I do not think that is the choice that we want to make. I think we all want to be protected from these horrific images, but we should be very careful that we do not say that we want to be protected from them and then say, “Oh no, we don’t want to know what you do on the internet.” That is the choice that we face, and we must have an open and honest debate about it.

I am not calling for there to be no legislation to deal with the problems of the internet, because clearly there are problems. We need to legislate to ensure that the internet providers are doing their very best to remove such horrific images, but we also need to have a much wider debate about our approach to the internet. We cannot have it both ways. I do not think it is the choice that we want to make. I do not think it is the choice that the Committee is making, but I do think that we need to be very careful about the choice we make.

dogs are being slaughtered every year for human consumption. In many countries, including the Republic of Korea, Vietnam, and Thailand, eating dog meat is a traditional practice. However, the consumption of dog meat has become increasingly popular in some countries, especially in China, as a status symbol and a perceived health elixir. As a result, the dog meat trade has exploded.

The trade in dog meat is particularly brutal and inhumane. Dogs are often captured, stolen or bought from pet shops. They are usually stolen from the streets or homes, and the methods used to capture them are horrific. They are chased down, beaten, trapped, and even drowned. The methods of slaughter are equally cruel. Dogs are often beaten, electrocuted, bludgeoned, and boiled alive, sometimes while still conscious. They are usually skinned alive, and their eyes are removed for consumption.

The dogs are frequently transported long distances, often in cramped, filthy conditions, with little or no food, water or ventilation. In some cases, dogs are confined in cages and transported in the back of trucks or in cars. The dog meat trade is also associated with other forms of animal cruelty, including the abuse of cats, monkeys, and other animals.

Dog meat consumption has been linked to a number of diseases, including rabies, leptospirosis, and tapeworm infections. In addition, the practice of consuming dog meat is associated with a number of social and welfare problems, including the theft of pets, the spread of disease, and the abuse of animals.

The Government are aware of concerns about the FA’s decision to host this tournament in Qatar. The UK Government have taken a number of steps to engage with Qatar on human rights issues ahead of the tournament. The Prime Minister has made clear that we expect Qatar to meet international standards of human rights, including on workers’ rights. Our ambassador to Qatar has raised the issue of migrant workers’ rights with senior Qatari officials and employers, and has emphasised that the UK expects Qatar to implement the recommendations of the international labour organisation and the Gulf cooperation council on labour migration. The UK has also provided technical assistance to Qatar to help the country reform its labour laws, including by working with the ILO to develop a national action plan on labour migration. The Government have also raised the issue of the treatment of the LGBT community in Qatar.

I hope that the hon. Gentleman will appreciate that the UK Government are taking a robust approach, and that this will be the subject of ongoing dialogue. I hope that this gives the hon. the construction costs were much higher than expected, and that is why the price was so high. However, they were awarded the contract in the first place because they were the lowest tenderer! And, the cost of the project was much higher than the client was expecting, but the client did not cancel the contract or seek a re-tender when the costs became clear.

And the contract was let under the EU Public Works Directive. The EU auditors were not interested in investigating the cost overrun. They just checked that the contract was awarded fairly, and that was enough for them.

The problem with this is that it creates a system where contractors can under-estimate their costs, and then ask for more money during the project. This is not a good situation, and it is a disincentive for contractors to properly manage their projects, because they can always ask for more money later. It is a way of gaming the system.

In addition, it creates a situation where the client is not getting good value for money. The client is paying more than they should for the project, and there is no accountability for the contractor for delivering the project within budget.

Overall, this is a bad situation. It is a failure of good project management, and it creates a system where contractors can game the system to get more money, and clients do not get good value for money. It is not in the best interests of either the contractor or the client, and it is not a good way to do business.

I will not repeat all the arguments I made in Question Period. I will focus on the situation of the members of the armed forces.

The Armed Forces Act states that any member of the Canadian Forces who, without lawful excuse, harms themselves is guilty of an offence. That is, the mere fact of hurting oneself is considered to be an offence and is punishable by the military justice system. The member does not have to be medically unfit or unable to perform his or her duties.

This legislation, which is over 100 years old, still applies to our soldiers, sailors and air force members. This is the only time in our country where a civilian committing an act of self-harm is not punished, but a member of the armed forces is.

This is unjust and we should correct it.

Some say that it is a question of discipline and that this is why soldiers are punished for self-harm. But this argument falls flat because soldiers are not punished for simply being sick or having a disability. It is only when they are unfit for duty that they are deemed to be subject to discipline.

However, when a member self-harms, he or she is not necessarily unfit for duty. In many cases, they continue to perform their duties. However, they are still subject to military justice.

When a person enlists, he or she swears an oath to the Queen and to the country. This oath includes the commitment to serve and to be ready to make the ultimate sacrifice. Our soldiers are prepared to die for their country. It would be unconscionable to charge them, to punish them, for trying to save their own lives.

The Armed Forces Act is based on the assumption that the military should have more power over its members than society does over civilians

I want to talk about three key themes that are central to this budget and to our Government's thinking, namely jobs and growth, fairness and the future. These three themes are closely interrelated. We want to encourage and support job creation, but we also want to ensure that jobs are good jobs, that we have a fair distribution of income and that the burdens are shared as fairly as possible. We need to be concerned about the future, to ensure that we are putting in place the structures to meet the challenges that lie ahead.

Jobs and growth is the central goal of this budget and our Government. We want to get people back to work, to grow our economy, to increase our productivity and to build a strong, sustainable economy for the future. We have been working on this since day one. We have a plan for jobs and we have implemented it. The plan is working. Since the Budget 2012, we have announced 62 projects under the Action Plan for Jobs, which has led to the creation of some 32,000 jobs. We have announced further projects since then, leading to further job growth. In the first nine months of this year, we have seen 38,000 jobs created. This is a 13 year high. The unemployment rate has fallen for eight successive months. We are making progress. The number of people unemployed is down 22,000 on this time last year and down 98,000 on the peak.

We are seeing job creation in every region of the country. The biggest increases in employment are in the west, the south-west and the north-west, and in counties such as Donegal, Mayo, Cork, Clare and Kerry. We are seeing increases in employment in Dublin and in the commuter counties,

The food industry has already started to adopt these innovative techniques and it is important that we ensure that they are subject to robust regulation. This Bill will help us take a strategic approach to the regulation of these new technologies in the food industry.

The Government’s position is clear that it will regulate new technologies in the food industry in a proportionate and evidence-based manner, ensuring that they do not mislead consumers. This Bill will help us deliver on that commitment.

There are already strict rules in place to ensure that food labelling is accurate and that food is not misrepresented to consumers. These rules will continue to apply to all food, including food that has been altered by new techniques.

The Bill will amend the existing EU rules that lay down the rules on food information to consumers, and will introduce a new category of food for the purposes of food information to consumers, known as a “novel food”. This new category will apply to food that has been subject to a new food technology, and it will require novel foods to be pre-notified and assessed for safety before they can be sold.

The Bill will also introduce new rules on the labelling of food that has been subject to a new food technology, to ensure that consumers are informed about the use of these technologies. What does the Multiculturalism Act do?

The Multiculturalism Act recognizes that all Canadians, regardless of race, ethnicity, religion, or place of origin, have the right to equality and equal opportunities. The act encourages the federal government to take steps to preserve and enhance multiculturalism in Canada.

This includes supporting ethnic, cultural, religious, and racial communities in promoting their identity and heritage, and encouraging the learning of official languages, as well as other languages spoken in Canada, in order to further multiculturalism.

Why is the Multiculturalism Act important?

The Multiculturalism Act is important because it reflects the Canadian identity as a multicultural and inclusive society, where all Canadians are valued and have a role to play.

The act is also important for fostering a strong, diverse, and resilient economy. According to Statistics Canada, 21.9% of the Canadian labour force was foreign-born in 2016. The act recognizes and supports the contributions of these workers and communities.

Furthermore, the Multiculturalism Act plays a key role in addressing issues of systemic discrimination and promoting social cohesion. It encourages the federal government to take steps to address issues of racism, discrimination, and social exclusion, and to promote a more inclusive and welcoming society.

What is the Multiculturalism Program?

The Multiculturalism Program is a funding program administered by the federal government that supports ethnocultural and religious communities in promoting their identity and heritage, and in addressing issues of racism, discrimination, and social exclusion.

The program provides funding to organizations and individuals for a range of activities, including cultural events, language classes, and community development projects.

The current position is that the Scottish Parliament and Scottish Government are subject to UK constitutional norms, including the conventions and constitutional customs, as well as the law. This means that the Scottish Government will seek to ensure that it acts within the constitutional norms in relation to the UK Parliament and Government, and that it takes account of the UK Parliament's role in relation to devolved matters and the need for it to be kept informed of devolved matters which may have UK-wide implications.

As a matter of constitutional fact, the Scottish Government and Parliament are subject to the UK Constitution, and it would be inappropriate for them to take a position which is inconsistent with the constitutional framework in which they operate. However, it is important that we seek to ensure that the Scottish Parliament and Government are treated fairly and that any UK-wide measures which are taken by the UK Government are compatible with the devolution settlement. This is a matter which goes beyond simple constitutional theory, as we have seen in the past with matters such as the House of Lords' amendments to the Scotland Act 2016, and it is one which requires a careful and considered approach.

In terms of the current constitutional framework, it is worth noting that the Scottish Government is subject to the Sewel Convention, which provides that the UK Government will not normally legislate on devolved matters without the consent of the Scottish Parliament. ## What Constitutes Distracted Driving?

Distracted driving is defined as any activity that diverts attention from driving. The primary categories of distraction include:

- Visual: taking your eyes off the road
- Manual: taking your hands off the wheel
- Cognitive: taking your mind off driving

## Examples of Distracted Driving

Distracted driving can take many forms, including:

- Texting or talking on a hand-held cellphone
- Eating or drinking
- Adjusting a navigation system
- Reading, including maps or emails
- Personal grooming, such as applying makeup
- Reaching for items in the vehicle
- Engaging in conversations with passengers

## ICBC’s Crackdown on Distracted Driving

ICBC has increased its enforcement of distracted driving laws in an effort to reduce the number of crashes caused by distracted driving. Distracted driving laws are enforced by the BC RCMP, the BC Conservation Service, and municipal police departments. Distracted driving laws include:

- A $368 fine for a first offense
- Three demerit points
- A $483 fine and six demerit points for a second offense in a 12-month period

## How to Avoid Distracted Driving

The simplest way to avoid distracted driving is to turn off your cell phone or put it out of reach while driving. Other ways to avoid distracted driving include:

- Set your GPS destination before you start driving
- Secure loose objects in your vehicle before driving
- Don’t eat or drink while driving
- Keep your eyes on the road and hands on the wheel

the case of voluntary contributions. It is important that employers understand the distinction between tips, gratuities and service charges, and ensure that all payments are treated in accordance with the law.

The law on tips, gratuities and service charges is set out in the Employment Equality Act 1998-2015 (“the Act”). There are provisions in the Act which regulate the payment of tips, gratuities and service charges, and set out the rights of workers in relation to these payments.

Tips are defined as “any payment made by a customer or client of an employer to an employee of the employer in respect of services rendered to the customer or client”. Gratuities are defined as “a payment made by an employer to an employee in respect of services rendered by the employee”. Service charges are defined as “a charge made to a customer or client of an employer by the employer in respect of services rendered by an employee of the employer to the customer or client”.

Under the Act, it is unlawful for an employer to make a deduction from any payment made to an employee in respect of a tip, gratuity or service charge, unless the employee has consented in writing to the deduction. In addition, an employer must distribute any tips, gratuities or service charges paid to it in accordance with the Act.

The Act provides that an employer must distribute tips, gratuities and service charges “in such manner as is fair and reasonable, having regard to all the circumstances of the case”. This means that an employer must consider a number of factors when determining how to distribute these payments, including the number of employees who are entitled to a share, the amount of the payment, and the nature of the work performed by each employee.

Prince Philip was born in Corfu in 1921, the youngest son of Prince Andrew of Greece and Princess Alice of Battenberg. He was educated in France, Germany and the UK, and in 1939, he enrolled at the Royal Naval College, Dartmouth. The Second World War was fast approaching, and Prince Philip was determined to do his bit. He served in the Mediterranean, Pacific and Atlantic, rising to the rank of commander. He met Queen Elizabeth in 1939, but they did not become seriously involved until 1946, when she was 21.

In 1947, the Princess announced her engagement to Lieutenant Philip Mountbatten, the Duke of Edinburgh. The wedding was held on 20 November 1947, and millions of people around the world tuned in to watch the ceremony. The wedding of the Duke and Duchess of Edinburgh was the first time a royal wedding was broadcast on television.

Queen Elizabeth and Prince Philip had four children together—Charles, Anne, Andrew and Edward. The couple were married for 73 years, and Prince Philip was the longest-serving consort in British history. Prince Philip was a devoted husband and father, as well as an inspirational leader, mentor and role model.

As the Duke of Edinburgh, Prince Philip took on a wide range of roles and responsibilities. He was the driving force behind the Duke of Edinburgh's Award, a charity which encourages young people to develop their skills, their confidence and their resilience. He was also a patron of over 800 organisations, including the Royal Society, the Royal Institute of British Architects, the National Trust and the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement.

But what is striking about this debate is that it was not about the principle of conscription, but rather about how that principle should be applied. Even when conscription was reintroduced, it was not simply in the form of general conscription for all men and women aged between, say, 18 and 60. Rather, the application of conscription was limited to a small number of key industries, with a range of exemptions and other qualifications.

The key question was about what, and who, was essential to the national interest in the context of a particular moment in history. In the case of the war, conscription was used to ensure that enough manpower was available for the army, navy and air force, as well as to ensure that enough of the country’s essential industries – steel, coal, and so on – could continue to operate.

In peacetime, the application of conscription was similarly focused on a narrow set of industries, with the key question being whether those industries were essential to the national interest, and whether there were enough people willing to work in them.

So the idea of conscription for women in the context of the reconstruction of the country after the war was not seen as a radical or revolutionary proposal, but rather as a logical extension of the existing system of conscription.

This year, as we mark the 75th anniversary of the liberation of Auschwitz, we reflect on the terrible events that took place at that camp and across Europe during the Holocaust. We think too of the many other communities and individuals who have suffered persecution, genocide and discrimination as a result of prejudice and hatred, from the Romas and Sinti to the Jewish community in Yemen.

We all have a part to play in ensuring such horrors are not repeated. We can start by challenging prejudice and discrimination wherever we see it, by standing up for what is right and fair, and by learning from the lessons of history.

We can also make sure that we are doing everything we can to support the Jewish community and other groups who are facing hatred and discrimination today, including through the work of the Holocaust Memorial Day Trust and the UK Government’s cross-government action plan to combat antisemitism.

As Holocaust Memorial Day takes place, let us remember the words of Primo Levi: “it happened, therefore it can happen again: this is the core of what we have to say. It can happen, and it can happen everywhere.”

If we are to truly honour the memory of the six million Jews who perished, and the millions more who have suffered in the Holocaust, then we must work to ensure that such atrocities never happen again.

As the Holocaust Memorial Day Trust say, “we must never forget; we must never allow the Holocaust to become a footnote in history.”

Cllr John Fuller
Leader of Waverley Borough Council

Every village had its vet, and it was a common sight to see him on his horse-drawn carriage, visiting the farms. In the summer, my father took me to the fields to help with the harvest, and we used to go to the farmyard at feeding time to feed the pigs and chickens. One day, when we were returning from the fields, we passed a small farmhouse on the edge of the village. We noticed a new, shiny car standing by the gate. As we walked on, I saw a large dog lying on the ground by the gate, with a broken leg, and a look of utter terror in its eyes.

My father turned to me and said, “That dog has been beaten. Let us go and help it.” I ran to the dog, and as I approached, I saw that the owner was coming towards us with a stick, and he shouted at me, “That’s my dog. Don’t you go near it.” My father said, “That is a cruel man. We will take the dog to the vet.” The man grabbed the dog by the collar and said, “I’ll take it to the vet myself.” But he didn’t. The paper describes the current approach to HTA in Ireland, the problems that have arisen in the implementation of new health technologies, and the need for change.

## Introduction

Health technology assessment (HTA) is a systematic and explicit analysis of the properties, effects, and relative value of a health technology. The process involves a detailed analysis of both the efficacy and cost-effectiveness of new health technologies and a judgement on their likely benefits in the Irish context. This analysis is used by the HSE to inform decision-making in relation to the introduction of new health technologies into the Irish health system.

The HSE, which was established in 2005, is the largest employer in the State and is responsible for the provision of health and personal social services. The HSE has established a Health Technology Assessment unit to guide the introduction of new technologies into the Irish health system.

The HSE and NICE then negotiate with industry regarding the uptake of new health technologies in the Irish health system.

The Consumer Protection Act 2007 (the “CPA”) provides that consumers are entitled to be given all relevant information concerning the goods or services purchased. The sale of tickets for above-sale-price is a breach of this requirement under the CPA.

If you have purchased a ticket online and the price is higher than the face value of the ticket, the CPA may apply. It is important to note that the sale of a ticket through an unauthorised seller does not mean that the sale is automatically invalid. However, if the seller is not authorised to sell the ticket, it is likely that the ticket will be invalid.

The CPA gives the consumer a right of redress in the event that they have suffered loss or damage as a result of the unauthorised sale of a ticket for above-sale-price. The consumer may bring a claim in the District Court and may seek an order that the ticket is invalid and the consumer is entitled to a refund of the money paid for the ticket.

I am going to deal with three issues in my contribution this evening. First, the present system of recruitment of judges in Ireland is flawed and does not guarantee the appointment of the best person for the job. Second, there is a significant lack of transparency in the present process, which undermines the confidence of the public in the judiciary. Third, the present system, with its requirement for a candidate to secure the support of their peers, can create an unhealthy and unhelpful culture in the legal profession.

The present system of recruitment of judges in Ireland is flawed and does not guarantee the appointment of the best person for the job. The process is carried out by the Judicial Appointments Advisory Board. There are 12 members of the board, four are appointed by the Government, four are appointed by the chief justice, two are appointed by the president of the High Court and two are elected by the legal profession. The board meets in camera to review the applications it receives and then to interview the shortlisted candidates. The names of the successful candidates are then put to the Government for appointment.

Deputy Gino Kenny also raised the issue of jobseekers being denied access to JobPath because they are considered to be in employment. The policy in this regard is that jobseekers who are in receipt of unemployment payments are deemed to be unemployed, unless they are in employment on a regular and continuous basis, in which case they are no longer considered to be unemployed. This is the policy currently in place, and the Department of Employment Affairs and Social Protection will continue to engage with the JobPath providers to ensure the policy is being implemented correctly.

The issue is the development of a national database of all State-owned and State-managed lands. I know it is an issue that has been raised before. I raised it on Committee Stage of the Land and Conveyancing (Amendment) Bill 2016, which was introduced by my colleague, Deputy Humphreys. It was raised again on Committee Stage of the Local Government (Planning and Development) (Amendment) Bill 2016. I will continue to raise it until the Government makes a decision on this issue.

This is not a partisan issue. I am not making it a party political issue. The development of a national database of all State-owned and State-managed lands, including the details of the landowner, location, size, zoning, planning status, etc., would significantly reduce the number of sites available for unauthorised development, improve the co-ordination of local authority development plans, simplify the planning system and ensure that the State and its agencies are contributing their fair share to meeting our housing needs.

We are in the midst of a housing and homelessness crisis. The Government has set targets to build 33,000 social housing units and 25,000 affordable purchase homes. It has not built enough homes to meet its targets. The Government's own figures show that the number of new social housing units has fallen by almost a third over the past year. There is no reason to believe the figures will improve in the near future. A national database of all State-owned and State-managed lands would make it easier for housing bodies, local authorities and Government agencies to identify sites and progress developments. It would also reduce the administrative burden on local authorities and the planning system as a whole.

It is important that we ensure that the collection and use of this sensitive information is carried out in a fair and transparent manner, and that our laws keep pace with technology. That is what Bill C-5 is about.

The bill would amend the Criminal Code and the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act to create a national DNA data bank. In a country like Singapore, there are so many stakeholders and modes of transport to consider. For instance, we have:

1. Ports
2. Roads and expressways
3. Rail networks
4. Sea and air freight services
5. Land transport services (buses and taxis)
6. Maritime and aviation services
7. Warehousing and storage facilities
8. Cold storage
9. Inland container depots
10. Terminals for freight handling
11. Customs and immigration services
12. Logistics companies
13. Courier services
14. Supply chain management companies
15. Government bodies (e.g., Singapore Customs, IRAS, LTA, MTI, etc.)

To make a change, I would need to understand the inter-dependencies between these stakeholders and modes of transport, and the impact they have on the functioning of the supply chains. To do this, I would appoint an independent commission to map out these supply chains comprehensively, so that we can make the best decisions for the future. I would also ensure that data is collected from various sources, including government agencies, businesses, and the public, to gain a complete understanding of how the supply chains operate.

We need to ensure that when we do invest in housing for First Nations communities, it is sustainable. That is why the Government of Canada has developed a framework for investing in housing for First Nations.

The framework focuses on the following three principles:

1. First Nations have the right to decide on their housing priorities and solutions.

2. First Nations have the capacity to lead and implement their housing initiatives.

3. The Government of Canada will support First Nations as partners and in a manner that builds on First Nations’ capacity and self-determination.

In 2016, the Government of Canada began working with First Nations to develop new housing investments. We have signed 81 funding agreements with First Nations to date, with a total investment of approximately $1.6 billion. We will continue to work with First Nations to develop new housing investments.

The First Nations Housing Strategy is a key part of our broader commitment to improve the quality of life for First Nations people. Our goal is to ensure that First Nations people have access to safe and affordable housing that meets their unique needs and supports their social and economic development.

The strategy provides a framework for federal investments in First Nations housing, and it recognizes that First Nations have the right to decide on their housing priorities and solutions. It is important to note that the strategy is not a one-size-fits-all approach. It recognizes that each First Nation is unique, with its own priorities and needs.

The strategy also acknowledges that First Nations have the capacity to lead and implement their housing initiatives. The Government of Canada will support First Nations as partners and in a manner that builds on First Nations’ capacity and self-determination.

The women of Canada have made a significant impact in our country's development. They have been trailblazers, innovators, leaders and activists. Today I want to recognize a few of the many women who have made significant contributions to this country.

Lady Franklin, wife of Sir John Franklin, was a tireless advocate for her husband and the crew of the doomed HMS Erebus and HMS Terror. In the face of widespread belief that her husband was dead and that no rescue was possible, she worked tirelessly to garner support for rescue missions and to locate the missing ships. In 1854, she published a book, The Fate of Sir John Franklin, to counter the belief that her husband's crew had perished. She also lobbied for her husband's knighthood to be restored and for a search for the ships to continue.

Dora Mavor Moore was a pioneering Canadian playwright, director and actress. She co-founded the Canadian Playwrights' Theatre in 1920, which later became the Stratford Festival. She is best known for her play, The Fool's Matrimony, which was produced by the Stratford Festival in 1953. It is still considered one of the most important Canadian plays of the 20th century.

In that situation, the landlord or agent would not be entitled to recover any of the costs of repairing the damage from the tenant.

However, if the damage caused to the property is the result of a contractual breach by the tenant—for example, if the tenant damaged a property by smoking in bed—then the landlord would be entitled to recover the reasonable cost of repairing that damage from the tenant. People who come to Canada as immigrants are subject to the immigration laws of Canada. They go through the process that we have established, which includes a medical exam, which includes a criminality check, and it includes a background check. We have very robust screening processes in place to protect Canadians, and there is no reason to think that they are not effective. They are effective, because the vast majority of people who come to Canada as immigrants are well-integrated and productive members of our society.

However, when it comes to those who come to Canada as asylum seekers, they are subject to the refugee determination process, which is a completely different process. That process is designed to protect individuals who, because of their political beliefs, their ethnicity, their race, their religion, or their membership in a particular social group, have been persecuted in their countries of origin.

I think it is important to clarify that distinction, because in both cases the safety and security of Canadians is the primary concern. However, the process for asylum seekers is different because of the purpose of their coming to Canada, and it is different from the process for immigrants, who come for the purpose of building a better life in Canada.

I think that was an important distinction to make, and I am glad I had the opportunity to do so.

Thermal runaway occurs when the electrodes—the part of the battery that stores the energy—heat up and then start to burn, releasing gases. This causes more heat to be generated, and the gases expand, which ruptures the battery case. The battery then continues to burn, and if it’s in a pack of batteries, the gases can spread to the other batteries and start them on fire, too.

The gases also contain lithium, a highly reactive metal that can react with other substances and lead to the production of more heat, which can cause the fire to propagate rapidly. For these reasons, lithium-ion battery fires can be difficult to extinguish and can result in substantial property damage. The question is: How can we prevent these fires from happening?

To prevent a lithium-ion battery from catching fire, you can take a few simple steps. First, avoid charging the battery when it is hot. This can cause the battery to degrade over time and increase the risk of thermal runaway. Second, avoid using the battery in extreme temperatures. Lithium-ion batteries should be stored and used at room temperature. Third, make sure the battery is not physically damaged. This can include punctures, cuts, or other signs of physical trauma. Fourth, avoid charging the battery too quickly. Fast charging can cause the battery to heat up and increase the risk of thermal runaway.

We are delivering more affordable housing than ever before. Over the next four years, Government will deliver 50,000 new affordable homes under the three new programmes – cost rental, social housing, and affordable purchase.

The Social Housing and Affordable Purchase programmes are progressing well with over 3,000 units in planning. The new cost rental programme is now delivering homes. The first cost rental developments have completed, and the first tenants have moved in.

The Cost Rent programme is a welcome change from the old rent-buy scheme. The rent for these homes is set by the Residential Tenancies Board (RTB), and is based on the market rent for similar homes in the same area. This means that the rent for these homes will increase annually in line with the consumer price index (CPI), but will not be subject to the annual rental caps set out in the Residential Tenancies Act 2004.

There are several advantages to the Cost Rent programme. First, the rent is set by the RTB, which ensures fairness and transparency. Second, the rent is affordable for families on middle to low incomes. Third, the rent is capped at 30 per cent of gross income, which means that the homes are genuinely affordable for families on middle to low incomes. Fourth, the rent is secure, with tenants only being required to give one month’s notice to leave, rather than three months notice as under the Residential Tenancies Act 2004.

The Cost Rent programme is just one part of the Government’s efforts to increase the supply of affordable housing. Tees Valley Mayor Ben Houchen has once again delivered a significant vote of confidence in the area's economy, as the Tees Valley Combined Authority has welcomed a multi-million-pound investment into the region by global aluminium giant Rio Tinto.

Rio Tinto will invest £360 million into the expansion of its Teesside Aluminium Smelter, which is a major part of the 4,000-strong workforce in the region’s £6bn aluminium sector, creating 100 jobs and safeguarding over 500 more in the process.

The investment will also support the development of Teesworks, the UK’s largest brownfield site, which is set to attract major companies and create thousands of new jobs in the coming years.

Mayor Houchen said:

“This is a massive vote of confidence in our region and our economy. We have a proud history of working with Rio Tinto, and this investment will not only create jobs but also support the growth of Teesworks, our flagship industrial site.

“Tees Valley has a wealth of experience in the aluminium sector, and with companies like Rio Tinto leading the way we can look to the future with confidence. We have a strong, growing economy, and we’re ready to show the world that Teesside is open for business and ready to welcome investment.

“Our work to secure this investment has not only demonstrated our strong relationship with one of the world’s leading industrial companies, but also our commitment to supporting the growth of the Tees Valley economy.”

The investment was announced at the Rio Tinto’s annual results presentation, where the global aluminium giant revealed its ambition to increase its global production of low carbon aluminium to 40% by 2030.

Fur farming is the practice of keeping animals, typically foxes, mink and raccoon dogs in cages for the purpose of breeding them for their fur. These animals are confined to small, barren cages for their entire lives, denied the most basic of their natural behaviours such as running, swimming and socialising.

Fur farming is also a cruel and inhumane industry that has been associated with numerous health risks for the animals, the workers and the wider public. The animals suffer from a wide range of diseases and conditions such as fur rot, mange and foot rot. Workers are exposed to a wide range of zoonotic diseases such as leptospirosis, campylobacter and salmonella which can pose a risk to public health.

In addition to the cruel treatment of animals, there is also a strong environmental argument against fur farming. The production of fur consumes vast amounts of water, energy and other resources. It is estimated that the production of a single fur coat can use up to 2,000 litres of water and 18.5 kilowatt hours of energy. This is a significant environmental impact for an industry that produces a luxury item that is worn by a very small percentage of the population.

The fur industry has also been linked to the illegal trade in endangered species. There have been numerous reports of illegal fur farms operating in countries such as China, Russia and the Baltic states. These farms often operate in secret and use endangered species such as the Siberian tiger, polar bear and snow leopard.

There is a growing trend towards the elimination of fur farming in Europe. The European Union has banned the sale and import of fur from animals bred and kept in cages since 2010. Several

I just want to tell you about my grandmother, who was born in India, in Peshawar, in 1922. Her family moved to Pakistan after the Partition and she lived there until she was 88. I would like to share with you something that happened to her and, in a way, to me, when she was 92.

My grandmother was a nurse, and she was always very proud of her work, as she should have been, because she did a lot of good things for people. She was a member of the Red Cross. One day, a few months before she passed away, she was sitting in her garden, reading her newspaper, when she suddenly heard the sound of a helicopter. She looked up and there it was.

It was a helicopter from the royal household. It landed, and out came Prince William and his wife, Kate, and they came to see my grandmother. It was such an extraordinary moment, but what moved my grandmother the most was that they asked her about her work and how she was feeling and, of course, she loved that.

A few days later, she received a letter from Kensington Palace with a photograph of my grandmother, Prince William and Kate, in her garden. She was so touched. That small gesture meant the world to her, because it showed that the royals cared about ordinary people, who they might meet on a sunny day in a garden.

I would like to thank Her Majesty for her reign and her devotion to the country, but also for showing us how a member of the royal family can relate to ordinary people, and how much of a difference it can make in their lives.

The CMS aims to provide a more efficient and child-centred service to families who are no longer living together and who have children. The CMS aims to ensure that children have a stable financial future after a family break-up by securing regular and affordable child maintenance.

The Child Maintenance Service will calculate the amount of child maintenance that should be paid by working out an assessment. This is based on the non-resident parent's income and the number of children that the resident parent is responsible for.

There are two ways in which parents can make arrangements for child maintenance to be paid:

If the parents make a private arrangement, the CMS can provide information on how to do this, but it will not become involved in the arrangement. If the parents cannot agree on the amount of maintenance, the CMS can calculate the amount that should be paid.

The review must take into account the equality impact of the Act on people with protected characteristics, which are age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex and sexual orientation.

The Secretary of State is required to consult with the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC), relevant public bodies, and other bodies as they consider appropriate.

The EHRC has the power to conduct its own review of the Act if it feels that the Secretary of State's review is not adequate. If the EHRC is not satisfied with the Secretary of State's review, it can issue a report to the Secretary of State setting out its concerns and recommending action.

In this debate we have heard much about the role of trade unions in protecting workers’ rights and advocating for fairer wages and conditions. But we have also heard about the role that trade unions play in creating a stable and fair workforce.

The role of trade unions is twofold: they are responsible for representing the interests of workers to employers and they are responsible for ensuring that workers are able to work in a safe and healthy environment. In order to perform these roles effectively, trade unions need to be able to act in the interests of their members without fear of legal repercussions. The increase in the limit on damages for tortious acts is a measure that is designed to provide trade unions with this protection.

The current limit on damages is set at $10,000. This limit was set in 1974, and it has not been increased since. Inflation has eroded the purchasing power of this limit, and it is now worth only about $45,000 in today’s dollars. The proposed increase to $250,000 would bring the limit in line with the purchasing power of 1974, and it would provide trade unions with the necessary protection to carry out their roles effectively.

This measure is supported by a wide range of stakeholders, including the Australian Council of Trade Unions, the Law Council of Australia, and the Australian Human Rights Commission. The Australian Council of Trade Unions has stated that the increase in the limit on damages is “a necessary step to ensure that unions can continue to represent workers effectively and without fear of financial ruin.” The Law Council of Australia has also expressed its support for the increase, stating that it is “essential for maintaining the proper functioning of the industrial relations system.”

I will set out in this statement the Government’s updated approach to the negotiations, which is based on our core principles. The question of dignity in assisted dying is a matter of great importance to many Canadians and to many members of the House. It is a matter of great importance to me, but my approach is different from that of my colleague. I have always believed that there is a need for an independent review of the Bill C-7, the Assisted Dying Act, and that review should take place within the first 12 to 18 months of its passage.

I think it is important to have that independent review to make sure that the legislation is working as intended, that it is not overly onerous and that the criteria for accessing the legislation are reasonable and achievable. This is a question of access.

There are cases in Quebec where individuals who meet the criteria for assisted dying have not had access to the service, and it is important to make sure that we are not creating a situation where the only people who will have access are those who have the means to pay for it.

As members have heard, the legislation requires that the individual making the request must be capable of giving informed consent. I think it is important to make sure that the information provided to that individual is accurate and complete, and that includes the information about the potential for alternative treatments or palliative care. Under section 60 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994, which is the power that has been used to allow the stop and search of people in Parliament Square during protests, such stop and search powers apply only to people who are in the area at the time. That means that, if the power were to be reintroduced—I will come to that later—only those people who are in the area at the time would be subject to such stop and search powers. It would not be open to the police to stop and search a Member of Parliament or a Member’s staff as they were coming to work. The power would be targeted at the people who are in the area at the time.

Under the Bill, the power would not be reintroduced for the entire Parliament Square area, but only for the designated areas where there has been a serious breach of the peace. The power is a response to disorder, and it is not there to be used in a general way against people in the area. I will come to that later, but it is not possible to use the power to stop and search Members of Parliament or their staff as they were going to work.

The work of the United Nations is crucial to bringing stability, security and development to those countries and regions most affected. The United Nations provides a platform for peace and dialogue, for humanitarian assistance, for political solutions and for sustainable development.

The UN has a vital role to play in working with the governments of countries, with civil society, with the private sector, and with people across the world. The United Nations also has a responsibility to work with Member States to strengthen and reform itself.

The United Nations is also in a difficult place. It faces financial challenges, it faces political challenges, and it faces challenges in terms of its effectiveness and its ability to meet the needs of the people it serves.

The United Nations has a responsibility to itself, to its Member States, to the people it serves, and to the world, to make the changes necessary to ensure that it can continue to fulfil its role and its mandate.

The United Nations is a multilateral institution, which means that it is based on the principles of consultation, consensus and cooperation. The United Nations is also a global institution, which means that it is based on the principles of universality, impartiality and objectivity.

The United Nations is also a political institution, which means that it is based on the principles of sovereignty, non-intervention and self-determination. The United Nations is also a humanitarian institution, which means that it is based on the principles of human dignity, human rights and human security.

The United Nations is a unique institution, which means that it is based on the principles of unity in diversity, inclusiveness and diversity. The United Nations is also a development institution, which means that it is based on the principles of sustainable development, poverty eradication and the promotion of the well-being of all people.

This month, Minister for Social Protection, Joan Burton, announced changes that will allow more people to continue to receive a medical card or GP visit card after they reach pension age. Under the changes, a person aged 66 or over can continue to get a medical card if their spouse has a gross annual income of less than €400 per week. A GP visit card can be obtained if the spouse’s gross annual income is less than €500 per week. Previously the income limits were €350 and €450 respectively.

The changes are effective from 1^{st} September 2014. The income limits will also apply to people aged 65 and over on incapacity benefits.

These changes will help many people to stay in work longer, without worrying about how they will afford healthcare.

Government is not prepared to face up to the real issues affecting our health service.

On Wednesday, the Minister for Health came to the House to defend his department's handling of the crisis in our hospitals. We were told that hospital overcrowding has increased by 168% in the past five years. We were told that on 6 December, there were 588 people waiting on trolleys for beds. That is an increase of 200% since 2011.

On that same day, there were 262 children on trolleys, 212 of whom were in the emergency department. It has been established that 50% of all children who are admitted to hospital come through the emergency department. This means that 106 children who went to hospital on 6 December had to spend their time on a trolley before they were given a bed. This is simply unacceptable.

On the same day, 262 children were on trolleys, but only 119 paediatric beds were available. We are told that there is no crisis in our health service, but that is simply not true. The crisis is clear for everyone to see. We are told there is no crisis, but a young girl was found dead in a trolley in the emergency department in University Hospital Limerick last week. Her death was completely preventable. This tragedy could have been avoided if the Government had acted.

Last week, the Government was forced to act. It was forced to take action on the issue of hospital overcrowding. The Minister for Health announced that 200 additional beds would be made available in the coming weeks. This was welcome, but it is only a short-term solution. The Government must do more. It must act now to end the crisis in our hospitals.

should self-isolate as a precaution? What is the impact on that child’s education and what can parents do?

Firstly, the school must have a plan for remote learning and it must be in place for every child from every year group. That is a legal requirement. It is important that this plan is shared with parents and that they understand what it entails.

Secondly, if a child is sent home, the school has to provide work for them to do from home. It can be hard for the school to know exactly what to do as circumstances vary. It could be that a child has to isolate for a week or two, or for a whole term or even longer.

The child’s work should be age-appropriate, it should be challenging but not overwhelming. It should allow the child to continue their education at home. If you are unsure about the work that the school is setting, talk to them.

If the work is too difficult, the school should be able to provide work that is more appropriate. It is important for the child to be able to do some work, but it is also important that it is work that they can do.

If the child is self-isolating for a long period, they may need additional help. The school should be able to provide that. It may be necessary for them to have a home tutor or for them to work with a teaching assistant. This should be discussed with the school.

If the work is not being provided, or if the work that is being provided is not suitable, you should speak to the school. The school has a legal duty to provide work for your child.

If the school is not doing this, you can make a complaint. You can also contact the Education Ombudsman, who can investigate the matter for you.

I know that I was worried about this, but I didn't realise that the level of anxiety and fear I felt was shared by so many.

If you've been following the news over the last couple of weeks, you'll know that the Government is proposing to change the voting age to 16, and that it will have its second reading in the House of Commons on Friday.

If you're a UK resident under the age of 18, then you're in the same boat as me - you're going to be denied the right to vote on a piece of legislation that could affect you for the rest of your life.

I'm not going to go into the ins and outs of why this is such a bad idea, because there are already countless articles explaining the reasons why.

What I do want to do, however, is share my thoughts on why I think this legislation will lead to more young people being homeless.

I am 17 years old. I am currently a student, but come September I will be in employment. I have been fortunate enough to have a stable upbringing, and I have no doubt that I will be able to find work.

I have friends, however, who haven't been so lucky. Friends who have been in and out of care, who have been homeless, who have struggled to find employment and who have been let down by the system on countless occasions.

I know that if this legislation is passed, there will be more young people like this who will struggle to find their way in the world.

Amendment No. 79 is a Government redraft of the noble Lord, Lord Strathclyde's, successful amendment in committee providing that any regulations made under sections 50, 57 and 72 shall be subject to the negative resolution procedure. The Government redraft changes the wording of the amendment in order to meet the concerns of the Joint Committee on Statutory Instruments. The Committee was concerned that the negative resolution procedure would not be suitable for certain regulations which might be made under the provisions, such as those implementing technical standards.

I understand the concerns of the Joint Committee on Statutory Instruments, but I do not agree that it would be sensible to require the affirmative resolution procedure for all regulations made under sections 50, 57 and 72. This would be burdensome and inefficient, and would not be in keeping with the spirit of the legislation which is to ensure that regulations are not overly prescriptive. As a result, I support the Government's redraft of the amendment in order to meet the concerns of the Joint Committee on Statutory Instruments while at the same time ensuring that the principles which underlie the legislation are preserved.

The bill is a direct result of the failure of the Government to plan for our energy needs. The Government has been relying on the promise of a surplus of renewable energy to meet the country’s electricity needs. However, this surplus never materialised.

Ireland has been suffering from electricity shortages for years and the Government has been scrambling to fix the problem. The Government’s solution is to procure additional electricity generation capacity from the private sector through EirGrid, the state-owned electricity transmission operator.

The Bill will allow EirGrid to procure the additional capacity needed to ensure that Ireland’s electricity network can meet demand over the coming years. This capacity will be used to provide back-up generation to address unplanned outages, and to address imbalances in the wholesale market.

The Bill is essential to ensure that Ireland has a reliable and secure electricity supply in the future. It is also a missed opportunity to reform the electricity market and to address the failed renewable energy policies that have led us to this point.

The approach to examinations will be broadly similar to that in previous years, but with some adaptations to account for the effects of the pandemic on students. The measures include:

For accredited grades, there will be no written examinations. Instead, schools will prepare a portfolio of evidence, which will be assessed by the school’s subject teachers.

- fair, transparent and impartial
- conducted in a manner that is efficient and proportionate
- accessible and affordable
- conducted in a way that promotes good faith and co-operation between the parties

that we still have a long way to go in terms of addressing poverty. Do you agree?

I would say that we have made significant progress in India, but there is still much to be done. Poverty levels have been reduced, but there are still millions of people living in extreme poverty. We must continue to focus on economic development, education, and healthcare to ensure that everyone has the opportunity to lead a dignified life. In addition, we need to address issues such as gender inequality, caste discrimination, and corruption, which continue to hold back progress.

One of the key challenges in addressing poverty in India is the vastness of the country and the diversity of its population. With over a billion people, India is home to a wide range of cultures, languages, and traditions, which can make it difficult to implement policies that are effective across the entire country. However, I believe that with a concerted effort and a focus on evidence-based policies, we can make further progress in reducing poverty and improving the lives of millions of Indians.

Another challenge is the fact that poverty is not just an urban issue, but also a rural one. Rural areas in India often have limited access to education, healthcare, and employment opportunities, which can trap people in a cycle of poverty. We need to prioritize investments in infrastructure, such as roads and irrigation systems, and provide support for small farmers to increase agricultural productivity and income.

In conclusion, while we have made significant progress in reducing poverty in India, there is still much to be done. We must continue to focus on economic development, education, healthcare, and infrastructure, and address issues such as gender inequality, caste discrimination, and corruption. With a concerted effort and a focus on evidence-based policies, I am optimistic that we can make further progress in reducing poverty and improving the lives of millions of Indians.

This is not a matter of political ideology. This is a matter of economic and social importance, and it is not a time for political games.

The Government’s Bill was drafted with the explicit aim of protecting the Irish economy and jobs, and I am glad that the Government’s approach has been supported by Sinn Féin.

The Government’s Brexit Bill ensures that the Irish economy remains open for business, and it helps to protect the supply chains that are essential to jobs and growth.

It also ensures that our key services, such as our financial services, remain competitive.

Fianna Fáil should have supported the Government on this issue, rather than trying to score political points and playing politics with our economy.

In the past few weeks, the Dáil has also been debating the issue of how Ireland should respond to the UK Government’s proposal for a Northern Ireland backstop.

Again, Fianna Fáil seems to be trying to play politics with this issue.

The UK Government’s proposal for a Northern Ireland backstop is a serious one, and it is one that the Taoiseach has engaged with.

The backstop is a contingency measure to avoid a hard border on the island of Ireland.

It is not an ideal solution, but it is one that would provide a guarantee that there would be no hard border and no return to a physical border on the island of Ireland.

This is not a matter of political ideology.

This is a matter of economic and social importance.

It is essential that we have certainty, and that we do not leave ourselves exposed to the consequences of a hard border on the island of Ireland.

that effectively exclude certain asylum seekers from the 1951 Refugee Convention. The clause provides that a person may be excluded from refugee protection if they were responsible for their own exile or if their entry was not “in conformity with the laws and procedures of the country of arrival.”

The exclusion of certain asylum seekers from the Refugee Convention is a very serious issue that goes to the heart of our obligations under international law. The Refugee Convention is designed to ensure that people fleeing persecution are protected, irrespective of how they entered a country. It is not the job of the Irish State to decide whether or not another State’s laws have been breached in relation to an individual’s entry into this country. That is the function of the relevant State’s courts and tribunals.

Clause 10 could potentially lead to a situation whereby asylum seekers who arrived by boat or by crossing a land border – as opposed to those who arrived in a more “conventional” manner – are treated less favourably than others seeking refuge in this country. This is a dangerous and deeply divisive approach to take. In this context, it is important to note that the 1951 Refugee Convention does not differentiate between asylum seekers on the basis of their mode of entry. Such differentiation has no basis in law and is not in line with international best practice.

The Council of Europe’s Commissioner for Human Rights has already raised concerns about the potential impact of Clause 10 on Ireland’s compliance with the Refugee Convention. The Government must heed these concerns and commit to ensuring that Ireland continues to uphold its international obligations in relation to asylum seekers, regardless of how they entered the country.

In 2014, the Joint Oireachtas Committee on Health and Children looked at the issue and recommended the Bill. The Minister for Children and Youth Affairs, Deputy Zappone, has made a commitment to introduce the Bill in the Dáil this year and that is very welcome. The committee's report and the Bill are very important.

The Adoption (Information and Tracing) Bill is about the basic human right of every person to know who they are. I am not seeking to demonise the adoptive parents. They have done an enormous service to the State and to a child who was in need of a home. They are not the ones to blame. The issue is about the right of the adopted person to know who they are. A recent decision by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) has added to the uncertainty surrounding the use of Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) for data transfers from the EU to the US.

In Data Protection Commissioner v Facebook Ireland Limited, Maximillian Schrems (Case C-311/18), the CJEU was asked to consider the validity of SCCs as a legal basis for transfers of personal data from the EU to the US where the data protection standards in the third-country do not meet the adequacy standard.

Although the SCCs were not struck down in the judgment, the CJEU has made it clear that they are only valid where it is considered that the data protection controls in place in the third-party country meet the adequacy standard. American data protection standards do not meet that standard. This is because the US does not have a federal data protection law. Instead, it has a patchwork of federal and state laws that are not considered to be adequate.

The CJEU has also clarified that, when assessing the adequacy of a third country’s data protection laws, the European Commission must conduct an assessment of the legal framework in that country and any limitations that might impact on the effectiveness of the data protection provisions in the SCCs.

In light of the judgment, the European Commission has now re-opened its adequacy decision for the US and is expected to assess whether American data protection laws are adequate under the new criteria set out by the CJEU. The member is quite correct to point out the government's commitment to ensuring the long-term sustainability of Canada's forestry sector. We know that the forestry sector is a vital part of our economy. Not only does it provide employment for hundreds of thousands of Canadians, but it also ensures that we can access the natural resources that we need to build the homes, infrastructure and other things that are important to Canadians.

As we have seen over the past few months, the forestry sector has faced some challenges, particularly in the softwood lumber industry. However, this government has been very active in working to ensure that the sector continues to grow and develop.

That is why we have taken a number of actions in recent months to promote the sector and ensure that it remains competitive. For example, we have increased funding for the Canadian Forest Service by 26%, which will allow the service to take on additional research and development projects.

We have also increased funding for the Canadian Wood Council, which promotes the use of wood in construction and helps to ensure that Canadian forest products are competitive in the global marketplace.

In addition, we have taken steps to support the softwood lumber industry, including through the establishment of the softwood lumber advisory committee, which provides advice to the government on how to best support the sector.

We are also working with our partners in the United States to find a long-term solution to the softwood lumber dispute. We believe that a fair and reasonable solution is in the best interests of both countries, and we are committed to working towards that goal.

Overall, the government is committed to ensuring the long-term sustainability of Canada's forestry sector. We know that the sector is vital to our economy, and we are taking action to support it and ensure that it remains competitive in the global marketplace.

I want to take this opportunity to speak to the issue of contact tracing and how it has been handled in this country. It is a very important issue. It is a vital tool for any country that is trying to manage a pandemic.

I want to explain some of the issues that have been raised and the information that has been provided by the Ministry of Health, and to also highlight some of the things that need to be done to improve the system.

First, I want to explain what contact tracing is. Contact tracing is the process of identifying, assessing and managing people who have been exposed to a communicable disease to prevent onward transmission.

It is a critical component of any pandemic response. It is the first line of defence against the spread of the virus, and it is the key to breaking the chain of transmission.

The World Health Organization has stated that contact tracing is "the cornerstone of the response to COVID-19".

In Trinidad and Tobago, the Ministry of Health has been using a contact tracing system that was developed by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO). This system is called Epi Info.

Epi Info is a software program that is used to collect, manage and analyse data related to public health events, including outbreaks of communicable diseases.

If the individual was not removed, they would simply be treated as a new applicant. That means that they would be entitled to access to public funds, and would be entitled to access to legal advice and representation, just as any new applicant would be.
