Galway, we are seeing homeless figures that are not being reported by the media and are not being highlighted by the Government. The Government are not being open and honest about the true scale of the housing crisis in Galway and in every other city and town across the country.

The latest figures released by Galway City Council show that there are 179 families in emergency accommodation in Galway, 104 of whom have children. In 2017, there were 169 families and 71 children in emergency accommodation. This means that the number of children in emergency accommodation has increased by 18 and the number of families in emergency accommodation has increased by 16. These figures are a disgrace and they are not being highlighted enough. I welcome the opportunity to speak on this issue because the numbers are rising every week, every month and every year.

There are 368 people in emergency accommodation in Galway. When we break it down, we see that 179 are families, 104 of whom have children. We also see that there are 189 individuals in emergency accommodation. There are 159 men and 30 women. When we look at the number of children in emergency accommodation, we see that there are 133 children in Galway City. When we look at the number of families in emergency accommodation in Galway County, we see that there are 76 families and 71 children. This means there are 209 children in emergency accommodation in Galway City and County. These numbers are a disgrace and I will not stand by and let this continue.

First, I will put on record my thoughts about what happened on 19 October, 1974. The right hon. and learned Member for Folkestone and Hythe (Sir Hugo Swire) was not in the House at the time, because he was not born, but I was. The Troubles were still going on in Northern Ireland, and they had been going on for a very long time. The Conservative Government had not managed to solve them. The Labour Government of 1974, of which I was a part, were trying to do so. Unfortunately, a bomb went off in the Brighton Grand Hotel, where the Conservative party was meeting. It was a very serious bomb, and it killed five people and injured 34.

The Conservative party was meeting in order to have a conference to decide who would lead it and who would become its Prime Minister. That bomb attack was designed, it appears, to kill not only those Conservative party members, but the Conservative leader, Margaret Thatcher. The Government, both the Prime Minister and the Home Secretary, were at the conference, but they were not harmed because they were in their rooms at the time.

However, one person was killed who was not a Conservative party member. That was WPC Yvonne Fletcher, who was on duty outside the Libyan people’s bureau in London, which was in St James’s Square. Her colleagues were trying to protect that building because of the IRA’s previous bomb attacks on it. A shot came from the Libyan people’s bureau and she was killed. That was a terrible day for her family, for the police and for the country.

The Government of Canada will continue to invest in innovation, research and the development of new technologies to support a strong and prosperous economy.

The Government of Canada is taking steps to ensure that all Canadians have the skills and training needed to take advantage of these opportunities. Through the Canada Training Benefit, Canadians will have more opportunities to learn, grow and adapt throughout their careers. That was set up because of the mining industry and the pastoralists that wanted to bring in migrant labour, but did not want Aboriginal people on their properties. The Protection Board was established to remove the children from their families, and that is what was happening in the 1960s.

I know that if I had been taken away, I would have thought, ‘What have I done wrong to be taken away?’ The children were not told anything. They were just told they were being taken away. That was the end of the discussion. They were taken away, and they would not see their families again for many years. Some children, as I have discovered, never did see their families again.

This process of reconciliation is so important because it is the healing process. The people who went through that experience of being taken away, and those who were left behind, were affected by it. The effects on the children, on those who were left behind, and on the whole communities, are still being felt today. It has had a ripple effect throughout the whole Aboriginal community.

One of the issues that we have to deal with is the fact that we have the highest rate of youth unemployment in the European Union. I am talking about the 25-24 age group, and that is something that we have to address. It is not something that we should shy away from or find too difficult or daunting to deal with.

One of the things that has been brought to my attention by a number of people is the issue of apprenticeships. I know there are a number of other issues with apprenticeships, in terms of the payment of the levy and the like, but what I am most concerned about is the issue of the number of apprenticeships that are available in this country. I recently had a meeting with a group of young people in the town of Fermoy, in County Cork, and I was shocked at the number of young people who were coming forward to say that they had qualified in a number of trades, in particular, carpentry and construction and electric work, and that they could not find employment. In many cases, they were not even being given the opportunity to go for an interview. In some cases, they were told they did not have enough experience, although they had done a full-time apprenticeship.

We have to address this issue in a practical way and in a realistic way. The Government needs to work with employers, particularly in the construction sector, to ensure that apprenticeships are available and that they are filled. The Government must also address the issue of the payment of the levy. We should be looking at it in a way that is realistic and that will not be a burden on the employers. The Government also needs to look at how we can attract people into the sector by making the apprenticeship schemes more attractive and more accessible to young people.

The member might be pleased to know that our government, unlike the previous Liberal government, has a plan for child care. The plan is based on three elements. The roadmap is based on five key pillars:

1. National leadership, governance and monitoring
2. Consumer education and awareness-raising
3. Business engagement
4. Food recovery and redistribution
5. Legislation and policy development

A number of key actions have been identified under each of these pillars. These actions will be implemented in a phased manner over the lifetime of the roadmap, which will run from 2022 to 2030. The roadmap will also include monitoring and evaluation mechanisms to ensure that progress is being made in reducing food waste.

The public consultation on the draft roadmap received a significant level of engagement, with more than 100 submissions received. Bill C-71 is not only about the short term. It is about addressing gun violence in the long term. I also think that the bill addresses the issue of handguns and the fact that there are too many handguns in the hands of too many people. We have seen that the measures contained in Bill C-71 are going to help us reduce gun violence in the long term. I am convinced that, when we look back in 10 or 15 years, we are going to be able to say that we have made a difference.

The long-term solution is always the best solution, because it is a solution that will have a lasting effect. It will allow us to prevent gun violence in the future.

The Government has set a target for the reduction of water consumption per person by 20% by 2020. To this end, the Water Services Investment Programme 2007-2013 provides for an investment of €4.8 billion in water services infrastructure. This programme focuses on the upgrading and expansion of water services infrastructure in the domestic, commercial and industrial sectors. The Government has also recently announced a further investment of €3 billion in water services infrastructure as part of the National Development Plan 2007-2013.

The Government has also taken a number of measures to address the problem of water leakage. For example, the Water Services (Amendment) Act 2007 requires water service providers to develop and implement water loss management plans to reduce water leakage. The Government is also working with the water services sector to ensure that water loss management plans are fully implemented.

The Government has also recently announced measures to tackle the problem of water pollution. For example, the National Wastewater Management Strategy 2011-2021 sets out a comprehensive strategy for the management of wastewater in Ireland. The strategy aims to improve the water quality of our rivers, lakes and coastal waters by ensuring that wastewater is properly treated before it is discharged into the environment.

We have set out our vision for a country where women and girls can live free from violence, abuse and fear. But we cannot achieve this vision alone.

We want to see the public, politicians, and the police play their part.

Our proposals will help to ensure that women and girls are protected and can live free from violence, abuse and fear.

1. Create a new domestic abuse statutory framework, including a duty for local authorities to commission a network of specialist domestic abuse services, and for police to prioritise the response to domestic abuse, including the use of covert technology to protect victims.

2. Increase funding for women's refuges and other specialist services for women experiencing domestic abuse, including a new fund to enable services to provide safe accommodation for children, as well as their mothers.

3. Establish a new Domestic Abuse Commissioner to ensure the consistent and effective response to domestic abuse by statutory agencies, and to provide an advocate for victims and survivors.

4. Create a new mandatory code of practice for employers to enable them to better support women experiencing domestic abuse.

5. Provide additional funding for schools and colleges to teach children and young people about healthy relationships, and to implement the Home Office's statutory guidance on domestic abuse and safeguarding.

6. Increase the use of Clare's Law, so that more victims of domestic abuse can be warned if their partner is a risk, and to provide additional support for those at risk.

7. Increase the maximum sentence for stalking to ten years, and introduce a new offence of "coercive control" to tackle the ongoing psychological abuse that can have a devastating impact on victims.

8. Introduce a new mandatory life sentence for murderers who have been convicted of a previous act of domestic violence.

## What are the best palliative care services in Australia?

The best palliative care services in Australia are those that:

1. Offer care that is patient-centred and delivered by a team of experts with a focus on the physical, emotional, social and spiritual needs of the patient and their family.
2. Are accessible and available 24/7, with a quick response time to referrals and requests for assistance.
3. Provide care in a variety of settings, including hospitals, hospices, aged care facilities, private homes and residential care facilities.
4. Offer a range of services, including pain and symptom management, psychological and spiritual support, and practical assistance with tasks such as feeding, bathing, and dressing.
5. Have a strong focus on communication and collaboration, working closely with other healthcare providers to ensure that the care provided is coordinated and effective.
6. Offer support for families and loved ones, providing information, emotional support, and practical assistance as needed.
7. Are committed to continuous quality improvement, regularly reviewing and updating their practices and procedures to ensure that they are providing the best possible care.

9. Are accessible and affordable, with funding and resources in place to support their work.
10. Are transparent and accountable, with clear policies and procedures in place for managing complaints and concerns, and a commitment to open and honest communication with patients, families, and the wider community.

But the S gene is the most important because that's the gene that codes for the protein that allows the virus to infect cells.

If the S gene is missing, it's unlikely to be as infectious or as lethal as other variants. But we don't know how infectious it is, and we don't know how lethal it is.

We also don't know how easily it transmits from person to person, how well it evades immune responses, or how well it evades vaccines. We're still in the process of finding out the answers to those questions.

The fact that it's missing the S gene does provide a glimmer of hope, though. It may mean that it's not as dangerous as some of the other variants, like delta. But it's too early to say for sure.

We'll have to wait for more data to come in before we can make any definitive conclusions about the transmissibility, lethality, and vaccine evasion of omicron. Canadians are rightly concerned about the increasing rate of violence and gun crime. In 2021, gun-related homicides in this country rose by 12% from the previous year, marking the fifth consecutive year of increases. The number of firearms incidents has increased by 18%. We have seen the tragic and senseless loss of life in our cities, with the most recent horrific mass shooting in London, Ontario, in which four members of the Afzaal family were killed, and the senseless killing of 22-year-old Jonathan Valleau in my hometown of Montreal, among many others.

This devastating trend can be linked to the rise of illegal guns on our streets. As I mentioned, in 2019, the Trudeau government lifted the long-gun registry, which was a crucial tool for law enforcement to trace the origins of illegal firearms. According to data from the RCMP, between 2008 and 2014, the long-gun registry provided 84% of all gun-tracing leads, while the handgun registry provided only 16%. The federal government's decision to scrap the long-gun registry was short-sighted and reckless, leaving law enforcement agencies in the dark when investigating gun crimes.

The problem of illegal guns is not limited to Canada's urban centres. In recent years, we have seen a concerning spike in gun violence in rural communities as well. In 2021, gun-related homicides in rural areas increased by 55%. In the first quarter of 2022, gun-related homicides in rural areas were up by 70% from the same time in 2021. The federal government cannot ignore this issue any longer.

Today, the Government of Canada is launching a Veterans’ Employment Strategy, a national strategy to provide employment support to veterans and their families. The strategy will create new opportunities for veterans to use their unique skills in the Canadian labour market.

As part of the strategy, the government is taking the following steps:

1. Creating the Veterans’ Employment Transition Program, which will provide employment services and career counselling for veterans, including pre-release employment support for those transitioning out of the military.
2. Providing employers with tools to hire veterans, including a new online portal, the Veterans’ Employment Network, and a national campaign to promote the hiring of veterans.
3. Enhancing and expanding the Veterans’ Independence Program, which provides employment support to veterans with disabilities.
4. Increasing access to education and training for veterans, including support for veterans to pursue post-secondary education through the Veterans’ Education and Training Benefit.

In addition to these actions, the government is also working with provinces and territories to expand employment supports for veterans.

I am proud to be a part of a government that is committed to supporting veterans as they transition out of the military and into civilian life. This strategy is a key step in ensuring that veterans have the opportunities and resources they need to succeed in the Canadian labour market.

## The waste hierarchy

The waste hierarchy ranks waste management options in order of preference from best to worst. The hierarchy is underpinned by the concept of waste prevention and the principle of the waste hierarchy, namely the waste hierarchy is the preferred approach to waste management. The waste hierarchy is a tool to support the sustainable management of waste and the promotion of waste prevention.

The waste hierarchy is incorporated into the Waste Management Act 1996 as follows:

- the waste hierarchy shall be applied in the planning and development of waste management facilities
- the waste hierarchy shall be the basis for the development of regional waste management plans

## Waste management planning

The regional waste management plans set out a vision, objectives and strategies for the sustainable management of waste in each region. The development of the waste management plans is based on the waste hierarchy and the waste management licensing requirements, including the requirement to carry out an environmental impact assessment for waste management facilities.

The regional waste management plans are reviewed and updated periodically. The latest iteration of regional waste management plans sets out how waste generated will be managed over the period 2019 to 2021.

The Government's decision to bring forward this Bill now is because of the need to ensure that the UK retains the ability to store and dispose of its own nuclear waste, as well as foreign waste, in the event of the UK leaving the Euratom treaty.

This is a necessary precaution in the event of a no-deal Brexit, which would mean that we would have to leave Euratom, or in the event that the UK and EU are unable to reach agreement on the terms of the UK's future relationship with Euratom by the end of 2020.

This Bill makes no change to the current legal basis for nuclear safeguards, which remains the Nuclear Safeguards Act 2000.

The Government will work to secure a future relationship with the EU on nuclear matters that ensures the UK's continued ability to store and dispose of its own nuclear waste, as well as foreign waste, and will ensure that our nuclear safeguards regime remains effective and efficient, maintaining the high standards of nuclear safety, security and non-proliferation for which the UK is renowned.

The ONR will continue to be the UK's nuclear safety and security regulator, with powers to ensure that operators of licensed nuclear sites meet our high safety and security standards. The Government will ensure that the ONR continues to have the necessary resources, both from Government and from the industry, to perform its duties effectively.

I would like to turn to the issue of the border. I believe that there is still a risk of a hard border in Northern Ireland in the event of a no-deal Brexit. The Secretary of State is right to emphasise that the UK Government are determined to avoid a hard border, but the EU position is that Northern Ireland must be treated as a third country and subject to third-country checks. The Minister of State, my right hon. Friend the Member for South West Wiltshire (Dr Murrison), has said that the UK Government do not believe that this is necessary, but I am not convinced. I have heard the argument that it is not necessary because Northern Ireland is part of the UK, and therefore there is no need for any checks on goods going from Northern Ireland to the rest of the UK. However, if the UK Government are going to allow goods to be imported into Northern Ireland from the EU without any checks, then they are breaking their own customs rules. That is what the EU would see. The EU would say, “You are allowing goods to come into the UK without any checks being made.” I am not convinced that the UK Government are prepared to accept the consequences of that.

As a result, I believe that there is a risk of a hard border. I do not think that it would be good for anybody. It would not be good for the people of Northern Ireland, it would not be good for the people of the Republic of Ireland and it would not be good for our businesses. I am sure that the Secretary of State agrees with me on that. If we are going to avoid a hard border, we need to have some form of agreement with the EU. I do not believe that the current Government have any intention of reaching such an agreement.

I am going to talk about the Home Office’s recent actions in relation to the Windrush Generation and the way in which some people were treated.

The Windrush Generation were invited to the UK in the post-war years to fill the labour gap left by soldiers. They came with the intention of staying for a short while, but many decided to make their lives in the UK, and have contributed to our society in so many ways.

However, as they did not have the right documentation to prove their right to remain, they have been in a state of limbo. Some have been threatened with deportation, some have been deported, and some have been unable to access services and employment because they have no documentation.

It is a scandal that people who have lived and worked in the UK for decades are being treated in this way, and it is clear that the Home Office has got it badly wrong.

Last week, the Home Secretary announced a review of cases of the Windrush Generation, which will be led by a former Permanent Secretary of the Home Office, and he said that no one will be removed from the UK unless it is safe to do so.

However, the damage has been done, and it is right that the Home Secretary has said that he will set up a compensation scheme for people who have been affected.

But compensation will not undo the harm that has been done. The Home Office needs to do more than that, and it needs to act quickly to reassure people that they are welcome in the UK, that they have a right to stay, and that their contribution to our society is valued.

The public transport system in this country is almost entirely run on diesel, with over 70% of public transport journeys in Ireland being made on diesel buses. With over half of Ireland’s carbon emissions coming from the transport sector, it is critical that we address this issue.

The report also highlights that the Government is not on track to meet its emissions targets. It is projected that the Government will fall short by 6 million tonnes of CO2 by 2020 and 22 million tonnes by 2030.

The Government’s National Development Plan includes €1.2 billion for new roads, yet it includes a mere €150 million for public transport projects over the next 6 years.

The report identifies that there is a €4.4 billion backlog in maintenance of roads, rail and public transport infrastructure. The report also notes that the lack of investment in public transport infrastructure and maintenance is leading to congestion and delays, and that these inefficiencies are costing us €3 billion annually.

The Green Party has consistently called for an increase in investment in public transport and active travel. We have called for a 10 year capital investment plan for public transport, with a priority on electrifying the rail network and replacing diesel buses with electric buses. We also support a network of protected cycle lanes and walking routes across the country.

In light of this report, it is clear that the Government’s current approach to addressing climate change is not working, and we need a significant increase in investment in public transport and active travel if we are to meet our emissions targets and address congestion in our cities.

I am proud that the Green Party is the only party that is committed to reducing emissions in line with what science demands and to building a sustainable future for Ireland.

As part of the Sláintecare reform agenda, a new national strategy for general practice will be developed, which will set out a comprehensive, coherent and ambitious vision for general practice in Ireland. The strategy will ensure the primary care sector is resourced to meet the needs of patients and communities now and into the future. The development of this strategy is a priority for the Department of Health and HSE.

The strategy will be informed by the work of the Sláintecare implementation team and the report of the independent primary care review, chaired by Dr. Rhona Mahony, which was published last year. It will also take account of the recommendations of the independent working group on general practice, which reported in February 2021. The working group was tasked with identifying the immediate steps that can be taken to address the current crisis in general practice, as well as making recommendations for long-term reform.

The report of the working group highlights the need for additional funding for general practice. In particular, it recommends that the budget for general practice should be increased to at least 12% of total health expenditure over the lifetime of the Sláintecare reform programme.

In addition, the working group makes a number of recommendations to improve access to general practice services, such as the expansion of out-of-hours services and the implementation of a national triage system. It also recommends measures to improve the working conditions for GPs, such as the establishment of a dedicated GP workforce planning unit and the development of a national framework for the recruitment and retention of GPs.

The report of the working group is being considered by the Sláintecare implementation team and the Department of Health, and we will work to implement the recommendations as soon as possible. The development of a new national strategy for general practice will be a key part of this work.

The government’s decision to invoke the Emergencies Act is therefore premised on the potential for the blockades to become threats to the security of Canada, not on the conclusion that the blockades themselves currently constitute such threats.

The invocation of the Emergencies Act is based on the existence of an emergency, which is defined in section 2 of the Act as an “urgent and critical situation of a national scope arising from an external or internal threat to sovereignty, security or territorial integrity of Canada.” The external or internal threat must be “of such a nature and of such magnitude as to seriously endanger the lives, health or safety of Canadians and to exceed the capacity or authority of a province to deal with it.”

The Federal Court of Appeal has previously stated that the term “emergency” requires “an extraordinary state of affairs, a crisis or a catastrophe.” The Act is meant to be invoked in extreme circumstances.

The government has argued that the blockades pose a threat to the security of Canada due to their potential to escalate into violence, cause economic harm, and disrupt the functioning of critical infrastructure. The government has also argued that the blockades pose a threat to the territorial integrity of Canada, as they are obstructing the movement of goods and people across the country, and that the blockades pose a threat to the sovereignty of Canada, as they are being carried out without the authority of the government and are challenging the rule of law.

The bodies of the children who died there were buried in a septic tank, and the exact number of children who died and were buried in the tank remains unknown.

Carbon capture and storage (CCS) is a vital technology for reaching net zero. It involves capturing carbon dioxide emissions from industrial processes and power stations, and then storing them underground in rock formations. This can reduce emissions by up to 90%.

CCS is currently used in a small number of industrial processes, such as the production of hydrogen and synthetic fuels. However, to reach net zero, we need to scale up CCS and apply it to power stations and other large emitters. This will create jobs and allow a just transition for the oil and gas sector.

I think what they are doing is a mistake. They are conflating administrative segregation with solitary confinement. They are not the same thing. I think they should be kept distinct. Solitary confinement should be abolished. It is a form of cruel and unusual punishment. But administrative segregation is a form of management.

My Lords, I thank the noble Lord, Lord Dholakia, for securing this debate on the Scottish Fiscal Commission’s report on Scottish devolution finances. I also thank all noble Lords who have contributed to the debate.

The Scottish Fiscal Commission’s latest report was published on 12 May. It provides updated projections for Scotland’s public finances under the Scottish devolution settlement. The report assesses the likely fiscal position of Scotland from 2021-22 to 2024-25. The latest report also includes forecasts for the period 2025-26 to 2029-30. The report’s projections are based on the latest economic data and the assumptions set out by the Office for Budget Responsibility in its March 2021 economic and fiscal outlook.

As noble Lords will be aware, the UK Government and the Scottish Government have different approaches to how they manage their fiscal positions. The Scottish Government have a significantly higher level of borrowing capacity than the UK Government, as they have greater flexibility over setting capital and revenue spending priorities, and can use reserve funds to respond to changes in the economic circumstances.

My riding has a strong agricultural sector, and as most people know, farm work is hard work. Farmers and farm workers face a number of challenges, including long hours, physical labour, and working in remote areas. However, they also face many of the same risks as workers in other sectors, including violence and harassment. It is important to remember that it is not only women working in large cities who are at risk.

The statistics are alarming. Statistics Canada reports that 30% of women in rural areas have experienced sexual violence, as opposed to 27% of women in urban areas. In 2017, 17 women were murdered in Canada. Of those, eight were from rural areas, and five were Indigenous women. In rural areas, these crimes often go unsolved, and survivors often suffer in silence.

Rural women and girls are often at higher risk for a number of reasons. They may live in remote locations, where resources, including legal resources, are less available. They may live in isolated communities, where support networks are not as strong. They may be concerned about losing their jobs, their livelihoods, or their communities if they speak out. They may fear the stigma of being a survivor of violence.

However, these women and girls are not alone. They have allies, and I am proud to be one of them. I am proud to have the opportunity to speak in support of Bill C-65.

Bill C-65 is an important piece of legislation that will help to create safer workplaces for all Canadians. It will strengthen the Canada Labour Code to ensure that federally regulated workplaces have policies and procedures to address workplace harassment and violence.

down. There are many forests in Canada, but there is one in particular that we would like to see protected, and that is the Boreal forest.

The Boreal forest is the largest forest ecosystem on the planet, covering about 300 million hectares, an area roughly the size of India. It is home to many rare and endangered species, many of which have already disappeared from other parts of the world. It is a vast wilderness that we cannot afford to lose.

The federal government has promised to protect 17% of this forest by 2011. If we are to meet this target, we must act now. Many provinces are working with the federal government to protect this valuable natural resource, but many have not. It is up to the federal government to ensure that all provinces are held accountable.

I urge all members of the House to support the Boreal Forest Conservation Act, which will give the federal government the authority to work with the provinces to ensure that the 17% target is met. This is a modest goal, but it will help to ensure that the Boreal forest remains intact for future generations.

I would like to take this opportunity to remind members of the House that the Boreal forest is the source of our clean air, our fresh water, our climate, and the habitat for over 90% of our birds. It is home to the caribou, the wolf, the moose, the bear, the lynx, the owl, the loon, and the beaver. It is the source of our national identity. It is the lungs of Canada, and we must protect it.

The time to act is now. I urge all members of the House to support the Boreal Forest Conservation Act and to ensure that this vital natural resource is protected.

In the case of the proposed amendments, the burden of proof would be reversed in respect of the humanitarian assistance defence. The prosecution would have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant was not acting for humanitarian assistance. The proposed amendments would ensure the burden of proof remains with the prosecution and would not unduly prejudice the right to silence.

There are some difficulties with the proposed amendments. The proposed amendments would not apply to any prosecution commenced before the Act comes into effect. This is because section 46 of the Act provides that it is not lawful to prosecute an offence under the Act before its commencement. The proposed amendments would only apply to prosecutions commenced after the Act comes into effect. This would provide an avenue of escape for the many arms traders who are currently being prosecuted for their actions in respect of the arms embargo on Sudan and who may be able to argue that their actions were for humanitarian assistance.

Section 6 of the Act is a general provision which provides that the Act applies to the supply of arms to Sudan. Section 7 of the Act is an offence provision which makes it an offence to supply arms to Sudan in circumstances where there is a reasonable belief that the arms will be used to commit serious violence in Sudan. This is the provision to which the proposed amendments refer. As the Deputy pointed out, section 7(2) of the Act provides that the offence shall be deemed not to have been committed where the person charged with the offence proves on the balance of probabilities that they acted for the purpose of humanitarian assistance. The proposed amendments would reverse the burden of proof to the prosecution.

It is important that we focus on this issue in the House and in the media, and that we have a national conversation about murdered and missing indigenous women and girls. I am proud that the NDP has been at the forefront of this issue for many years.

Indigenous women and girls make up 4% of the female population in Canada, but they account for 16% of the female homicides and 11.3% of the missing women. This is a crisis, and it is a crisis that disproportionately affects indigenous women and girls.

Indigenous women are more likely to be victims of violent crimes, including sexual assault, than any other group of women in Canada. They are more likely to be subjected to physical violence, and they are more likely to be victims of murder. This is a crisis that must be addressed.

This is new section 43A of the Sexual Offences Act 2003 (as amended by the Criminal Procedure Act 2017) that comes into force on 1 October 2017. The new provision sets out the procedure for making an application under Part 36 of the Criminal Procedure Rules for leave to ask questions or to adduce evidence about a complainant’s sexual behaviour. The new section includes a number of requirements for the court to consider before granting leave, and provides for the complainant to be informed and to make representations about the application.

The new provision is part of a wider reform of the criminal justice system aimed at addressing the problem of complainants being asked about their sexual history in rape trials, which can be distressing and can affect the credibility of the complainant in the eyes of the jury. The new section is intended to prevent such questioning unless it is necessary and proportionate in the circumstances of the case. The new provision is a welcome development and is likely to be of significant benefit to complainants in rape trials.

The Northern Ireland protocol Bill is a piece of legislation that could have been drafted by a schoolboy. It is a mess, and it is an attack on the United Kingdom. The protocol is not only illegal under international law—which I have explained to the Government—but it is also unworkable and undemocratic. The Secretary of State is correct in saying that it is unacceptable and undesirable for Northern Ireland to be treated differently from the rest of the United Kingdom.

The protocol threatens the political stability of Northern Ireland by giving the European Union a veto over the decisions of the Northern Ireland Assembly and the United Kingdom Parliament on matters such as taxes and immigration. It will also mean that there will be a hard border in the Irish sea, with checks on goods moving from Great Britain to Northern Ireland. There will be a cost to the taxpayer of hundreds of millions of pounds to set up new infrastructure and to administer the protocol. That cost will be borne by the British taxpayer, not the European Union. The protocol is also an attack on our sovereignty.

The Government have said that they will be seeking a renegotiation of the protocol with the European Union. I believe that there are six key areas that the Government must insist upon in that renegotiation: the first is that the European Union must scrap article 13, which allows for the European Court of Justice to have jurisdiction in Northern Ireland. The second is that the European Union must ensure that there will be no checks at the Irish sea. The third is that the European Union must ensure that the United Kingdom can control its own laws and taxes in Northern Ireland, and not be subject to the EU’s state aid rules.

This is known as ‘the grant of planning permission with conditions’. Planning permission will be granted only in such a way that the character and appearance of the structure, as it was at the time of designation, will be preserved. This is known as ‘preservation by condition’.

It is important to note that the designation of a building as a protected structure does not affect the ownership of the property or the use to which it is put. It is not intended to interfere with the normal commercial activity of an owner, as it is recognised that changes may be necessary from time to time.

The designation of a protected structure means that the building is afforded protection from unauthorised alteration or demolition. Planning permission is required for any works which affect the exterior of the building or which are within the curtilage of the building, including the demolition or removal of a structure. The planning authority has the power to grant permission for the works which are necessary for the conservation of the building, or to allow alterations which are necessary for the proper use of the building or the adaptation of the building for another purpose.

In addition to the controls on development, the Planning and Development Act also provides for the issue of ‘restrictive covenants’, which may be attached to the title of a protected structure. These may restrict the types of works which can be carried out or the materials which may be used.

Local authorities are obliged, under Part IV of the Planning and Development Act, to prepare a Register of Protected Structures and to make that register available for inspection. This legislation is about removing the potential for tax evasion and the misuse of the common tax base. It is not about creating more red tape or extra burdens for small businesses. We are dealing with a very specific issue, which is about the misuse of the VAT system. As Members of the House will know, a VAT number is the key to the VAT system. If one has a VAT number, one can claim VAT back on inputs, but if one does not have a VAT number, one cannot do so. There are many situations where one needs a VAT number, such as when buying goods from other EU Member States or when making purchases in a retail context.

The issue we are dealing with today is that some businesses do not want to have a VAT number because of the potential liability to pay VAT. In this context, they are in effect using other businesses as a front. They ask these other businesses to register for VAT so that they can benefit from the VAT system without having the liability themselves. That is what this legislation is all about.

The legislation is simple. It is an amendment to the VAT Consolidation Act 2010 which will be inserted after section 32. It will provide that where the Revenue Commissioners believe that a business is being used as a front by another business and where there is a concern that VAT is not being paid or is being under-recovered, the Revenue Commissioners will be able to seek information from the taxpayer about the nature and extent of the transactions it has entered into with the third party, the taxpayer who is the front.

The agreement says that Northern Ireland will remain in the customs union and single market, and the UK will align with those rules.

It does not mean that the UK will align with the whole of the EU’s regulatory and legislative framework. The customs union and single market are two different things. Customs union means you have a common external tariff and a common internal tariff, and you don’t do customs checks at the border between member states. The single market means that you have free movement of goods, services, capital, and people.

In the case of the Northern Ireland protocol, the UK will have to align with certain rules to ensure the seamless flow of goods and services between Northern Ireland and Ireland, and between Northern Ireland and the rest of the EU. This is to prevent a hard border on the island of Ireland, which would be detrimental to the peace process. It is not the same as the UK aligning with the entire EU regulatory and legislative framework.

It is not my intention to engage in any personal attack on the Taoiseach. I do not wish to question his commitment to public health or his work as a doctor. He was, as he has said, a junior doctor, but it was a different time.

In the 1970s and 1980s, the Department of Health and the HSE were not at the forefront of protecting patients’ rights. However, things are different now. We have legislation and regulations that put the patient at the centre of healthcare. It is also important to acknowledge that the Taoiseach was a junior doctor in the 1970s and 1980s, when things were different.

However, the issue here is not the Taoiseach’s past but the standards he is setting for the present. I will set out the facts of the matter.

The Taoiseach, as a junior doctor in 1978, removed the spleen of a 44-year-old patient, Mr. Michael Gallagher, without that patient’s consent. I believe that is the Taoiseach’s admission. He has said that the operation was carried out to remove a tumour but has not said that Mr. Gallagher gave his consent to the operation.

The Taoiseach removed Mr. Gallagher’s spleen without his consent. It is important to note that the operation was carried out without the Taoiseach having requested the patient’s consent. I do not know what role, if any, the patient’s family had in the decision.

The Taoiseach removed Mr. Gallagher’s spleen without his consent. He has said that it was a routine operation. However, a number of people have suggested to me that removing a spleen is not a routine operation

but it is important to do so in a way that ensures that all the vulnerable are protected. It is a difficult balance to achieve.

In addition to the capital works programme, the Government has also developed a Flood Risk Management Framework, to support the implementation of the Plan and ensure that all flood risk management actions are well co-ordinated, effective and sustainable. The Framework will be published later this year.

The Government is also committed to addressing the issue of flooding in a sustainable and climate-resilient manner. The NAF includes a range of specific actions in relation to flood risk management.

As the Deputy will be aware, the Government has already announced the development of a new strategic port in the Shannon Estuary to cater for increased freight traffic. The port will be developed in two phases. Phase 1 will involve the development of a deep water berth to accommodate larger vessels, along with associated infrastructure. The port company has already started the preparatory works for this development, which will be completed in 2023. The Shannon Foynes Port Company has also identified a number of potential investors to develop the Phase 2 infrastructure to develop the port into a major gateway port.

The new strategic port in the Shannon Estuary will provide a significant economic boost to the Mid-West region, as well as providing an alternative port to Dublin, should it come under pressure from Brexit. The port has excellent connectivity to the national road network and the M7 and M18 motorways will provide the necessary links to the ports at Dublin and Belfast.

In addition to the Shannon Estuary, I am also aware that the Port of Cork has also identified an opportunity to expand capacity and develop a deep water berth at Ringaskiddy. The Government has made €54 million in funding available for this project, which is expected to create over 1,000 jobs and have an economic impact of €1.2 billion.

As I have said, the Government has also provided funding for a number of other strategic port projects, including the development of a deep water port at Belmullet, Co. Mayo, and the development of a deep water berth at Greystones, Co. Wicklow. These projects are all part of the Government's strategy to ensure that Ireland has the necessary port infrastructure to cater for increased freight traffic in the future.

The rural area of South Gloucestershire, in which I represent, includes a part of the Cotswold Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty. It has a high number of small villages, but no towns. It is an affluent area with a high concentration of second homes. Rural crime is a serious issue, and it is not uncommon for the police to be called out to deal with incidents of theft, vandalism, arson, burglary, and violent assaults.

CCTV systems in rural areas have been shown to be effective in reducing crime, but there are significant disparities between towns and villages. In the town of Kingswood, the local council has recently installed 26 new CCTV cameras, as part of an upgrade. By contrast, the neighbouring village of Olveston has no CCTV system at all. There are other villages with CCTV, but the numbers vary widely. In my own village of Cheddar, the system consists of two cameras covering the main road and the local supermarket.

There are many reasons for this disparity. Councils often do not have the resources to fund CCTV systems. In many cases, funding is provided by the police, but their budgets are also under pressure. Some councils are reluctant to install CCTV because of the associated costs and the need to comply with data protection laws.

In addition, there is a debate about the effectiveness of CCTV in reducing crime. Critics argue that it can deter potential offenders, but it can also lead to a false sense of security. Some argue that it is only effective when combined with other measures, such as increased police patrols and better lighting.

However, the lack of CCTV in rural areas is a particular concern. In many cases, the police are stretched thin and are unable to respond quickly to incidents.

On May 12, 1923, Doris O'Connor was born in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan. After working as a nursing aid for several years, she attended the Saskatoon General Hospital School of Nursing.

Doris graduated as a registered nurse in 1948, and she began her career at the Saskatoon General Hospital, where she worked in various departments including pediatrics, surgery, and the surgical recovery room.

In 1954, Doris left Saskatoon for a new opportunity in the Northwest Territories, where she worked at the Whitehorse General Hospital for three years. She then moved to Winnipeg and continued her work in nursing, primarily at the Grace Hospital, where she worked for 26 years.

During her career, Doris also served on the nursing board of Manitoba and was a strong advocate for continuing education for nurses.

In 1991, Doris retired from nursing. In 1994, she moved to Qualicum Beach, B.C., to be closer to her sister. She continues to be active in her community and is a wonderful role model to her family, friends, and fellow members of the community.

In 1998, Doris received the Order of the Red Cross of the Holy Sepulchre from the Catholic Church in recognition of her service.

To Doris, and to all of Canada's nurses, thank you for your service and for the compassion you bring to the lives of Canadians every day. Happy International Nurses Day.

Unfortunately, the current law is that a legal collective agreement can be ignored by employers. The Employment Court has ruled that an employer has the power to terminate a legal collective agreement and unilaterally change any term of the agreement, even terms regarding wages.

The reason this is such an important issue is that it means that workers can be left high and dry. In a number of cases, employers have been found to have broken the law by ignoring legal collective agreements, but have still been able to avoid paying workers their agreed entitlements by simply breaking the agreement and not paying.

At present, workers are only able to get redress for breach of a collective agreement by taking the employer to court, which can be time-consuming and expensive. This is something that should not be necessary when the employer is in breach of a legal agreement.

The law should be changed to ensure that workers can have the same legal protections as other creditors, and that they can enforce their entitlements in the same way. This would make it much more difficult for employers to avoid their obligations, and would ensure that workers are treated fairly and receive the wages and conditions they are entitled to.

In addition, the law should be changed to allow workers to take collective action when their legal collective agreement is breached, rather than having to take individual legal action. This would give workers more power to enforce their rights, and would make it easier for them to take action when their employer is in breach of the agreement.

Overall, the law needs to be changed to ensure that workers are treated fairly and are able to enforce their entitlements in the same way as other creditors. This would help to ensure that workers are able to get the wages and conditions they are entitled to, and would make it more difficult for employers to avoid their obligations.

The cost of the proposed nuclear power station has risen dramatically due to a number of reasons: construction delays, increased safety requirements, and the rising cost of materials such as steel and concrete. Additionally, the station's design has undergone significant changes, with the addition of advanced safety features, which have increased the overall cost.

Furthermore, the decommissioning and disposal of nuclear waste is a significant ongoing cost that needs to be factored into the equation. The waste generated by a nuclear power station is highly radioactive and requires secure storage for thousands of years. This cost is not included in the initial construction cost, but is a significant ongoing expense.

In comparison, fossil fuel sources, such as natural gas and coal, have lower upfront costs and are less expensive to operate. They also do not require the same level of ongoing waste management and disposal costs as nuclear power.

In summary, while nuclear power can generate a large amount of electricity, the high construction costs, ongoing waste management costs, and the potential for cost overruns make it a less economically viable option compared to fossil fuel sources. It's important to carefully consider these costs when evaluating the feasibility of nuclear power projects.

It is important to remind the House of the scale of the issue. The number of abortions in England and Wales has fallen by 27% since 2001, with just over 190,000 abortions in 2016. That is a reduction of more than a third since 1990 and more than half since 1980. As other Members have said, the decline in the number of abortions is broadly consistent with the fall in teenage pregnancies. The Government have worked hard to improve sex and relationship education, which has made a significant difference. However, we must do more, because the fall in the number of abortions is not uniform across the country. The North-west has the highest number of abortions, and the south-east has the lowest.

What is the reason for the geographical variation? That is not fully understood, but the available evidence suggests that, as elsewhere in the UK, a number of factors are involved. In the North-west, for example, there are higher levels of deprivation, lower levels of educational attainment and higher rates of teenage pregnancy. The available evidence also suggests that the number of abortions is higher among people who are less well off, less well educated and in poorer health.

In 2012, the Public Health Minister at the time, the right hon. I will not speak to the bill in the detail that the hon. member has, but I want to touch on a few points that he did not have an opportunity to address.

The bill would amend the Criminal Code to provide that a person who, for the purpose of committing an offence, is in a vehicle that is being driven, is deemed to be driving the vehicle, whether or not he or she is actually in control of the vehicle. The bill would also amend the Highway Traffic Act to provide that a person who is deemed to be driving a vehicle under the Criminal Code is subject to the same penalties as a driver who is actually in control of the vehicle.

The bill was introduced in response to a Supreme Court of Canada decision in the case of R. v. Le, which held that a person who was in a stolen car that was driven by another person was not guilty of the offence of theft of a motor vehicle. The court held that the person was not driving the vehicle. The court's decision was based on the fact that the person was not in control of the vehicle. The bill would overrule that decision.

The bill would address situations such as the one described in the case of R. v. Le and other situations where a person, while not in control of a vehicle, contributes to the commission of an offence by being in the vehicle.

I want to be clear that the bill is not about people who are in the vehicle for no other reason than to ride in it. It is about people who are in a vehicle for the purpose of committing an offence.

The European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 provides for the transposition into domestic law of existing EU obligations and the continued application of EU regulations and decisions. The Agriculture Bill 2020 makes provision for a domestic framework for agriculture and the environment after the end of the transition period on 31 December 2020.

The first instrument amends the Common Agricultural Policy (Single Payment Scheme) (Great Britain) Regulations 2015, the Common Agricultural Policy (Greening) (Great Britain) Regulations 2015 and the Common Agricultural Policy (Cross Compliance) (Great Britain) Regulations 2015 in order to ensure that these are operable.

The second instrument amends the Organic Products Regulations 2009, the Organic Production (England) Regulations 2010, the Organic Production (Scotland) Regulations 2011 and the Organic Production (Wales) Regulations 2011 in order to ensure that these are operable. It also amends the Common Agricultural Policy (Organic Farming) (Great Britain) Regulations 2016 to provide for a 3-month extension to the deadline for submitting applications for conversion from a non-organic to an organic farm, in order to take account of the fact that farmers may not be able to meet the existing deadline due to the impact of COVID-19.

Both instruments have been made using the powers conferred by section 7 of the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 and come into force on exit day.

It will then take place, and the changes will be implemented at the next general election after that, which must be held by January 2031.

That is a long time to wait, but it is a compromise. It will allow us to make sure that the next review is fair and comprehensive, while minimising the disruption to communities. During this pause, we will keep the system under review to ensure that it continues to work effectively. If we need to make any further changes, we will bring forward further legislation.

Algorithmic systems are becoming increasingly complex and opaque, and they are being used in many different areas of Government, from deciding which applicants should be interviewed for jobs to deciding whether people should be granted bail or parole. The review that I am advocating would ensure that the algorithms used by the Government are designed to be fair and transparent, and that they take account of the diversity of our society. It would also ensure that there are checks and balances in place to ensure that algorithms do not make decisions that are inappropriate or discriminatory.

The review should be led by an independent expert, and it should include representatives from a wide range of sectors, including academia, technology, the legal profession, and civil society. The most obvious difference is that the economic free market determines resource allocation based on supply and demand. If the demand for a good is high and the supply is low, the price goes up. The next most obvious difference is that the economic free market is an attempt to create an optimal allocation of resources based on the wants and needs of people. In the water domain, the allocation of resources is determined by the political power of the various user groups, regardless of the wants and needs of the people. The wants and needs of the people are completely ignored. The allocation of water resources is based on political power, not human needs or wants.

It is constantly changing as new technologies are developed, new goods are produced, and new markets are created. In the water domain, the allocation of water resources is fixed. As a former member of the Defence Forces, I am proud to contribute to this important debate on the reports of the Minister for Defence regarding service by the Defence Forces with the United Nations in 2017 and 2018. I also wish to pay tribute to the men and women of the Defence Forces who have served and continue to serve our country with distinction and professionalism around the world.

The Defence Forces have a long and proud history of service with the United Nations. From the United Nations Emergency Force, UNEF, in the Suez crisis in the 1950s to peacekeeping operations in Bosnia, Cyprus, Haiti, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Mali, our soldiers have demonstrated courage and commitment in the service of peace and humanitarian objectives. Our service personnel have also shown great skill and expertise in the field of engineering, medical and logistical support to United Nations operations, playing a vital role in the delivery of essential services to communities in crisis.

I will now outline the key activities of the Defence Forces with the United Nations in 2017 and 2018. In 2017, a total of 1,313 personnel served on United Nations peacekeeping missions, including MINUSMA in Mali, UNIFIL in Lebanon, MONUSCO in the Democratic Republic of Congo and UNMISS in South Sudan. This represented a decrease of 188 personnel from the previous year. This decrease was largely due to the drawdown of the Irish Battalion from UNIFIL in Lebanon in the second half of the year, as well as the return of the Irish Battalion from MONUSCO in the Democratic Republic of Congo in the first quarter of the year.

To clarify, there is no such thing as “carbon capture” – we cannot capture carbon. We can, however, lock it away. This is what we mean by carbon sequestration. It is the process by which atmospheric carbon dioxide is removed and stored for long periods in materials such as soil, wood, and stone.

Carbon capture and storage (CCS) is a process where carbon dioxide is captured from power plants and industrial facilities and then transported and stored in geological formations, such as depleted oil and gas reservoirs or saline aquifers.

As we are all learning, carbon is not the only greenhouse gas. Methane has a global warming potential 28 times greater than carbon dioxide over a 100-year period and 84 times greater over a 20-year period. Methane is the second largest contributor to global warming after carbon dioxide. Agriculture is the biggest emitter of methane and it is imperative that we reduce its output.

To do this, we need to reduce methane emissions from livestock and manure management. We also need to reduce methane emissions from rice production and landfill, among others. The good news is that if we reduce methane emissions by 45 per cent, it could be equivalent to taking 85 per cent of current cars off the road.

This is what we must do. I am happy to report that I have had the honour of working with some fantastic companies, including one of the world’s largest food companies, that are implementing projects to reduce methane emissions from livestock and manure management.

We need to be bold and ambitious. We need to take action now. We need to do this together.

I wish to speak to Bill S-204 from a human rights perspective and highlight the importance of ensuring that all Canadians are protected from human rights abuses, including those related to the illegal organ trade.

First, let me address the fundamental human right to life, health and dignity. All human beings have the right to life. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in 1948, affirms that “everyone has the right to life, liberty and security of person.” The same principle is enshrined in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

The right to life also means the right to health and dignity. The World Health Organization's constitution, also adopted in 1948, states that the enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of health is one of the fundamental rights of every human being. This means that all Canadians have the right to live a life free from preventable diseases and health issues.

In addition to the right to life, we have the right to dignity. Article 5 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights states that “no one shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.” The right to dignity means that we have the right to be treated with respect, to be free from humiliation and to have our autonomy protected.

Now, let me turn to the human rights issues surrounding the illegal organ trade. The illegal organ trade is a grave violation of human rights. It involves the exploitation of vulnerable people, often from poor or marginalized communities, who are coerced or tricked into selling their organs for transplant. These organs are often harvested in unsanitary conditions, without proper consent, and without any regard for the donor's health and well-being.

The grant is also dependent on the student’s course of study. The grant is also dependent on the student’s course duration. For example, a student studying a three-year course will receive a grant for the duration of their course, while a student studying a four-year course will receive a grant for the first three years of their course.

The grant is also dependent on the student’s living arrangements. For example, a student living at home with their parents will receive a higher grant than a student living independently.

## Introduction

A key component of any response to a pandemic is testing, to identify infected individuals, trace contacts, and thereby reduce onward transmission. In the context of COVID-19, the UK government has faced significant criticism for delays in the development and deployment of testing capacity, but has since taken steps to increase the number of tests available, as well as the number of people tested.

In this article, we will examine the role of testing in the UK’s response to the pandemic, discuss the types of tests that are available, and consider the factors that have contributed to the UK’s current position in relation to testing.

## The role of testing in the pandemic response

Testing is a crucial component of any pandemic response. Testing allows infected individuals to be identified, which in turn can inform public health interventions, such as contact tracing, isolation, and targeted quarantine. In addition, testing can help to guide decisions about the need for interventions at a population level, such as school closures, business closures, and travel restrictions.

In the context of COVID-19, testing has also played a role in allowing some people to return to work, as well as in facilitating international travel. Furthermore, testing can help to inform research into the epidemiology of the virus, as well as the development and deployment of vaccines and therapeutics.

One option could be to require airlines to test passengers before they are allowed to board their flight, as they would be the only ones who can guarantee that passengers are tested at the right time, and can also enforce the testing requirements. This would also help to address the issue of passengers arriving in the UK with a false test certificate.

Another option could be to introduce more stringent checks at the airport, such as requiring passengers to present their test certificate at the airport before they are allowed to check-in, and implementing random testing for passengers to ensure compliance.

It is not fair to put at risk the health of the majority of travellers who are following the rules, for the sake of a small minority who are not.

Hormone Replacement Therapy is a group of therapies that replace and/or supplement one or more of the hormones made by the ovaries. The most common form is oral oestrogens and progesterone, but there are also patches, gels, creams, tablets and implants. HRT can be used to treat symptoms of the menopause, and to prevent osteoporosis. It is usually started around the time of the menopause and continued for five years, but may be continued for longer depending on the woman’s risk of osteoporosis and her symptoms.

Oestrogen is a hormone that controls the development and maintenance of female sexual characteristics. It plays a part in the menstrual cycle and is necessary for a woman to become pregnant. Oestrogen also affects the skin, hair, bones, heart, brain, liver, and other organs. Oestrogen levels fall during the menopause, which can result in symptoms such as hot flushes, night sweats, mood changes, and vaginal dryness. Progesterone is a hormone that prepares the uterus (womb) for pregnancy. It also helps to regulate the menstrual cycle.

HRT works by replacing the oestrogen and progesterone that the body is no longer producing. This can help to relieve symptoms such as hot flushes, night sweats, and vaginal dryness. It can also help to prevent osteoporosis by maintaining bone density.

There are some risks associated with HRT. These include an increased risk of breast cancer, blood clots, stroke, and heart disease. However, these risks are generally small, and the benefits of HRT usually outweigh the risks for most women.

means that there are times when it’s hard to make good choices.

There are also times when drinking can be part of a more complex picture. For example, drinking can be a coping strategy for people who are dealing with stress, anxiety or depression. There are also many reasons why people drink. People may drink to relax, to escape from difficult situations, to fit in with the crowd, to celebrate, to feel confident, to boost their mood or to feel more sociable.

Alcohol can have a negative impact on our health, our relationships, our work and our safety. The more you drink, the greater the risk of harm. The harm associated with alcohol can be immediate – for example, injury, violence, poor sexual decision-making and accidents – or it can be long-term, for example, alcohol dependency, liver disease, mental health problems and cancer.

However, the amount of alcohol a person drinks and the harm it causes are not always in proportion. This means that a person can have a high level of alcohol-related harm without having a very high level of drinking.

This is because harm is influenced by a range of factors in addition to how much a person drinks. These factors include the way a person drinks (for example, binge drinking or drinking to excess), a person’s tolerance to alcohol, the context in which a person drinks, a person’s gender, the health and wellbeing of a person, and their ability to cope with life’s challenges.

It’s important to remember that it’s never too late to make a change. Small changes can make a big difference and help you feel better about yourself.

The Minister for Finance, Paschal Donohoe TD, has today published the Statutory Instrument (SI) which will allow the annual general meetings (AGMs) of credit unions to be held virtually. The SI is titled the Credit Union Act 1997 (Covid-19) (Amendment) Regulations 2020.

This SI has been published by the Minister for Finance following consultation with the Central Bank, the Department of Employment Affairs and Social Protection, the Department of Rural and Community Development and the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage. The SI will be signed by the President shortly and will then come into effect.

In light of the COVID-19 pandemic, the Minister for Finance has been working closely with the Central Bank to ensure the continuity of the financial services provided by credit unions. The Government has also committed to introducing a suite of measures to support credit unions in the current environment.

The Central Bank has issued guidance to credit unions in relation to the holding of AGMs virtually, in line with the Public Health advice in relation to social distancing. This guidance can be found at the following link: https://www.centralbank.ie/regulation/credit-unions/credit-union-guidance-and-bulletins/covid-19-guidance/covid-19-guidance-for-credit-unions

The City of Toronto’s new Pandemic Response Standard (the “Standard”) came into effect on August 19, 2021. The Standard applies to all businesses and organizations that are considered “critical” under the City’s current classification system. The Standard is mandatory and must be followed by all covered businesses and organizations, as well as their employees and customers.

The Standard is being developed by the City and will be updated regularly to reflect the current public health guidance. The City has not yet published the details of the Standard, but it is expected to include requirements for businesses and organizations to implement measures to prevent the spread of COVID-19, such as:

* Implementing physical distancing measures
* Requiring employees and customers to wear masks
* Conducting regular cleaning and disinfecting
* Providing hand sanitizer stations
* Implementing capacity limits
* Requiring employees and customers to stay home if they are feeling sick
* Implementing contact tracing procedures

The City has not yet announced the timeline for the consultation or implementation of the Standard. It is expected that the City will provide more details in the coming weeks.

The Standard will be enforced by the City’s Public Health Inspectors, who have the authority to issue fines for non-compliance. The City has not yet announced the amount of the fines.

The City has not yet announced the timeline for the implementation of the Standard, but it is expected that it will be implemented as soon as possible.

The carbon tax was a revenue-neutral tax, meaning the revenue from the tax was to be returned to British Columbians. In this case, it was returned through tax credits to individuals and businesses. Those tax credits were calculated to be the same as the carbon tax, so in theory, the tax did not increase the total revenue of the government, but just shifted it from general revenues to the carbon tax.

However, the NDP government changed that and now the carbon tax is actually increasing the revenue of the government. The carbon tax is a consumption tax, so it hits the lower and middle income people hardest, because they spend a larger share of their income on consumption. The tax does not raise a lot of revenue, but it is a regressive tax and hits the lower and middle income people hardest.

We have to be very careful about consumption taxes, because they hit the lower and middle income people hardest.

Here is what the BC government did to revenue neutrality, and here is the impact on British Columbians.

The BC government removed the revenue neutrality of the carbon tax in the 2017 budget and now the carbon tax is increasing general revenues. The carbon tax increased from $30 to $35 per tonne in 2018 and will increase to $50 per tonne by 2022.

The table below shows the impact on a typical family of four, based on the BC Ministry of Finance’s calculations.

In 2018, the carbon tax will increase by $5 per tonne, and the average family of four will pay an additional $32.50 in carbon tax. However, the carbon tax credit will increase by $15.00, so the net increase for the average family of four will be $17.50.

The Withdrawal Agreement is a legally binding treaty under international law. The Bill purports to alter that treaty in a way that would be considered a material breach of international law, the Government’s own legal advisers have said that the Bill would be in breach of international law, and the Supreme Court has confirmed that Parliament can legislate to breach international law if it chooses to do so. The Bill does not provide for any dispute resolution mechanism as per Article 16 of the Protocol. Instead, it confers the power on the UK Government to unilaterally vary the Protocol at any time, and without any obligation to involve the EU. The UK Government has not even attempted to justify this breach of the Withdrawal Agreement, and the lack of a dispute resolution mechanism means that it will not be subject to any democratic oversight or scrutiny. The Bill also risks damaging Northern Ireland’s position in the single market, as the EU has already made clear that it will not renegotiate the Protocol on a unilateral basis. This Bill is an act of bad faith that breaches the UK’s international obligations, and risks damaging the UK’s international reputation and its standing in the world.

The Government has made a few moves to address the cost-of-living crisis, including increasing the national living wage to £9.50 an hour and providing a £200 discount on energy bills. However, these measures have been overshadowed by the fact the Government is not implementing the measures that Labour has been calling for, including the Windfall Tax on energy companies and a plan to cap energy bills.

The Prime Minister has been advocating for a windfall tax for some time, but the Chancellor has been against it. The Chancellor said: “A windfall tax is not the right answer. It doesn’t help households today, it doesn’t help us invest for the future. It’s a short-term cash grab.” This is despite the fact that it would raise over £5bn for the Treasury and could help to cap energy bills.

As I have said before, a windfall tax would not be a silver bullet, but it would be an important part of a comprehensive package to help people cope with the cost-of-living crisis. I am not convinced that the Chancellor’s alternative approach of increasing capital gains tax would do as much to help people with their bills.

The Government has also failed to take decisive action to address the problem of Universal Credit. Last year, the Government ended the £20 uplift to Universal Credit that was introduced during the pandemic. This means that the amount of Universal Credit someone receives is based on their circumstances in 2015, rather than 2022. This means that the amount of Universal Credit someone receives is simply not enough to live on, with many people struggling to put food on the table and keep a roof over their heads.

I am grateful to the hon. Member for Caithness, Sutherland and Easter Ross (John Thurso). He asked why we are not having a debate on the detail of the Bill. As I have said, I am happy to have an opportunity to debate the detail of the Bill, and I will do so in the coming weeks. It is not possible to discuss all the detail in a Second Reading debate, but I will have an opportunity to discuss it.

The hon. Member for Caithness, Sutherland and Easter Ross asked about the definition of a digital service. That is an important point, and I will give the House some detail on that.

We have defined digital services for the purpose of the Bill as services that are provided wholly or partly online. The digital services that the Bill covers are those that are provided by businesses to consumers, and include online platforms, social media, streaming services, online marketplaces, search engines and cloud storage services.

The Bill creates an age-appropriate design code that requires online service providers to consider the impact of their services on children and to take steps to ensure that their services are safe and appropriate for them. The code will require online service providers to provide age-appropriate settings, take appropriate steps to ensure that content, services and functions are safe and suitable for children, and provide meaningful and accessible information to children and parents on the use of their services and the measures in place to protect children.

The Bill also creates a new regulator, the regulator for children and online safety, which will have the power to issue enforcement notices to online service providers that breach the code and to impose substantial fines for non-compliance.

The maternity benefit will also be paid from the 26th week of pregnancy. The current system has a waiting period of 14 weeks. This means that mothers will receive maternity benefit from an earlier stage, when they may need the financial support.

The bill will also make some improvements to the parental leave benefit. The new rules will make it easier for parents to share the leave between them. Currently, one parent can take the entire leave, or both parents can take leave concurrently, but not consecutively. Under the new rules, parents will be able to take the leave consecutively if they wish to do so, provided that the total leave taken does not exceed the maximum amount.

- The introduction of a national passenger assistance scheme that guarantees every passenger assistance, whether they have a disability or are elderly.
