- The provision of real time information on all aspects of public transport, including accessibility information.

The European Council has also proposed a cap on the price of gas. This is a welcome measure, as it will help to protect consumers from excessive price increases. In this context, the recent announcement by the Government of a proposed carbon tax is both perplexing and unhelpful. The Government has said that this tax will be ‘revenue-neutral’, meaning that it will be offset by reductions in other taxes. However, this is a misnomer. It is a new tax, and it will have an impact on the cost of doing business in Ireland.

The proposed carbon tax will initially apply to fossil fuels and will increase annually at a rate of €7 per tonne, with an annual review of the rate. This tax is intended to discourage the use of fossil fuels and to encourage the use of renewable energy sources, as part of a wider strategy to reduce carbon emissions and combat climate change.

The Government has argued that the carbon tax is necessary because Ireland is not meeting its carbon emission reduction targets. While it is true that Ireland has been struggling to meet its targets, it is also true that the proposed carbon tax is not the most effective way to address this issue.

Firstly, the carbon tax will disproportionately impact lower-income households. This is because the cost of energy is a larger percentage of their income than it is for higher-income households. A recent report by the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) found that the carbon tax will have a regressive impact on household income, with the poorest 20% of households bearing a higher burden than the richest 20%.

Secondly, the carbon tax will have a negative impact on the competitiveness of Irish businesses. This is because our competitors in other countries will not be subject to the same carbon tax. For example, Germany has a carbon tax, but it is much lower than the proposed Irish tax, and the UK does not have a carbon tax at all.

Sharks have inhabited our oceans for over 400 million years, and they play a critical role in maintaining a healthy marine ecosystem, particularly as apex predators. However, human activities, primarily overfishing and the illegal shark fin trade, have led to a dramatic decline in shark populations around the world.

The demand for shark fin soup is primarily driven by its perceived status as a luxury dish, with the fins of certain species being highly prized, particularly the fins of the white shark and the shortfin mako. The process of removing the fins is horrific, with sharks being caught, their fins removed while still alive, and then discarded back into the ocean to die a slow and agonising death. This practice is not only inhumane, but it is also unsustainable, with many species now threatened with extinction as a result.

The impact of shark finning on our oceans is far-reaching. Sharks are critical to the health of marine ecosystems, and their decline can have serious consequences for other species. For example, the removal of top predators from an ecosystem can lead to an increase in the numbers of smaller, less desirable species, such as jellyfish, which can in turn disrupt the food chain and have a knock-on effect on other species.

Moreover, sharks play a crucial role in the carbon cycle, as they help to regulate the populations of other species, such as plankton, which are important for absorbing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. The decline in shark populations can therefore contribute to climate change

The Government’s intention in introducing the Bill is to maintain the UK’s open and welcoming approach to foreign investment, while ensuring that the security and resilience of our critical infrastructure are protected. In doing so, we are following the lead of many of our closest allies, including the United States, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, who already have similar powers and who have used them to intervene in cases where they believed that the national security or public interest of their countries might be at risk. It is important to note that this Bill will not in any way affect the vast majority of foreign investment in the UK. It will not apply to the many thousands of companies that are investing in the UK, creating jobs and contributing to our economy every day.

The Bill will provide the Government with the power to review transactions where they involve a foreign investor buying a controlling stake in a company that owns or controls critical infrastructure. It will also give the Government the power to review transactions that involve the acquisition of a controlling stake in a company that is already critical infrastructure.

The Bill does not affect existing powers to deal with national security threats. It is about ensuring that we have the tools to deal with foreign investment in a way that is proportionate to the risks posed. The Bill will include a number of safeguards to ensure that the powers are used in a way that is transparent and accountable. It will establish a register of notifiable acquisitions and will provide for a public notice process for transactions that are subject to review. It will also require the Secretary of State to publish an annual report on the operation of the scheme and to lay before Parliament a copy of each decision made under the Bill.

The purpose of the Bill is to establish a new statutory scheme for the accommodation and support of persons seeking international protection in Ireland. The Minister has stated that the Bill will provide for the replacement of the existing direct provision system, which will then be discontinued. It is designed to facilitate a more streamlined approach to the system of accommodation and support for persons seeking international protection in Ireland.

The Bill will amend the International Protection Act 2015 to provide for the establishment of the International Protection Accommodation Service, IPAS. IPAS will be responsible for providing accommodation and support to persons who are seeking international protection and are not in a position to provide for themselves. It will also provide a new administrative appeals process for appeals in respect of decisions of the Refugee Appeals Tribunal on applications for international protection.

The Bill also establishes the Office of the Appeal Commissioner, which will be responsible for the hearing of appeals and for the making of recommendations to the Minister in respect of those appeals. The Office of the Appeal Commissioner will replace the Refugee Appeals Tribunal.

In addition, the Bill will amend the Immigration Act 2004 to provide that the International Protection Appeals Tribunal will have jurisdiction to hear appeals against decisions of the Office of the Appeal Commissioner in respect of applications for international protection.

The Bill provides for the regulation of the accommodation and support provided by IPAS. It provides for the establishment of a new statutory scheme that will set out the rules and standards in respect of accommodation and support provided by IPAS. The Minister has stated that the new scheme will be more flexible and that it will take account of the varying needs of those seeking international protection.

We are all aware of the need for a balanced and coherent housing policy, and I am glad to see that the Government have taken steps to encourage the development of more affordable housing, such as the extension of the right to buy to housing association tenants, but I have to say that I still have some concerns. The Government’s approach appears to be to give home owners the right to buy, and to leave it to the market to solve the problem of affordable housing for those who do not own their own homes. I know that the Government have put some money into affordable housing, but the figures that I have seen suggest that this money is not nearly enough to solve the problem, and I hope that the Minister will address that issue in her response.

The right to buy was originally intended to allow people to buy a home of their own. I understand that the Government’s intention is to allow people to do that, but there are some difficulties with that. I have seen research that suggests that people will not always use the right to buy to buy a home of their own. For example, they might want to sell the home they have bought to a property developer who can afford to pay a higher price, or they might use the right to buy to buy a smaller property and rent out the house that they have vacated. If the Government’s intention is to increase the number of homes available for sale, the right to buy might be an ineffective way to achieve that objective.

I also have concerns about the effect that the right to buy will have on the supply of affordable housing, particularly in London and the south-east. I know that the Government have made some changes to the rules to try to address that issue, but I still have concerns about the impact that the right to buy could have on the supply of affordable housing in London and the south-east.

The European Union (EU) is a political and economic union of 28 member states, which are located primarily in Europe. The EU operates through a system of supranational institutions and intergovernmental negotiated decisions by representatives of the member states. It is the largest trade bloc in the world, with a GDP of approximately €18.5 trillion (US$23.4 trillion) in 2016. It was created in 1993 from the European Community (EC), which was itself created in 1957 by the Treaties of Rome.

The EU has developed an internal single market through a standardised system of laws that apply in all member states in those matters, and only those matters, where the countries have agreed to act as one. EU policies aim to ensure the free movement of people, goods, services and capital within the internal market, enact legislation in justice and home affairs and maintain common policies on trade, agriculture, fisheries, and regional development.

The EU’s aim is to attract and sustain high levels of foreign investment, while also ensuring that investment is sustainable, ethical, and compliant with national and EU law. It has also developed policies on trade, competition, and industrial issues, and has signed a series of free trade agreements (FTAs) with other countries and trading blocs. The euro is the official currency of 19 EU member states.

The EU has developed an extensive system of external relations, representing its member states in the international arena. The EU has been a major donor of foreign aid and has provided assistance to the developing world.

This is not a social welfare scheme, but an employment support service.

There are two contractors for JobPath – the Public Employment Service (PES), which is the Department of Social Protection, and the Private Employment Service (PES), which is a private company that has been awarded a contract by the Department of Social Protection.

JobPath offers a tailored employment support service to individuals on the Live Register who are long-term unemployed (15 months or more). The aim of JobPath is to improve employment outcomes for long-term unemployed individuals and reduce long-term unemployment. It provides participants with the opportunity to access supports to progress towards employment, education or training.

JobPath is a personalised and intensive employment support service which helps participants to identify their skills, build their CV, search for jobs, prepare for interviews and find a job.

The service is available to participants for a period of 12 months. If a participant is not employed at the end of 12 months, they can still access the JobPath service for a further 6 months, subject to continued eligibility.

To be eligible for JobPath, a person must:

- be aged 21 or over
- be in receipt of an Irish Social Welfare payment (or their partner is)
- have been signing on for 15 months or more (or their partner has)
- not be engaged in employment, education or training for the period immediately prior to commencing on JobPath
- be in receipt of a payment at a level in line with the eligibility criteria for the payment
- be living in the catchment area of the Public Employment Service or Private Employment Service, as relevant

Therefore, I have been concerned that the Westminster government has decided to impose an abortion regime on Northern Ireland that reflects the views of the majority of MPs in Westminster, but not the majority of people in Northern Ireland. It is particularly frustrating given that the people of Northern Ireland have had to wait years for decisions about the law on abortion to be made by their own assembly.

In April 2019, the Northern Ireland Executive published a proposal for reform of the law on abortion. This proposal was based on extensive public consultation, and was supported by a majority of MLAs in the Assembly. This proposal was delayed by the Westminster government.

In the event, the decision on abortion has been taken in Westminster, and I do not support the approach taken by the Westminster government.

In particular, the decision to remove the offence of procuring a miscarriage has been taken by the Westminster government, despite the fact that this offence has not been used to prosecute any woman in Northern Ireland in recent years.

I am also concerned about the way that the Westminster government has imposed this legislation on Northern Ireland without giving the people of Northern Ireland the opportunity to vote on the issue.

I do not believe that it is right for the Westminster government to impose its will on the people of Northern Ireland in this way. I believe that decisions about the law on abortion should be made by the people of Northern Ireland and their elected representatives.

One solution is to offer more support to women who want to take on leadership roles. This could include mentoring, networking opportunities, and leadership development programmes. We also need to challenge the stereotypes that prevent women from taking on leadership roles.

Another solution is to make leadership positions more flexible. This could include offering part-time positions, job sharing, and flexible working arrangements. This would make it easier for women to balance their work and family responsibilities, and would help to address some of the barriers that prevent women from taking on leadership roles.

We also need to ensure that we are providing positive role models for girls. The problem with political correctness is that it is a means of controlling people’s behaviour, making it conform to a particular orthodoxy. It is a means of excluding people and making them feel excluded. It is a means of making people feel that they are not part of the mainstream because they do not fit the prescribed stereotype. That is not a positive aspect of our politics.

We have to be careful that we do not replace one problem with another. A problem with the quota system is that it can be seen as a means of achieving a particular political objective by the back door. The quota system is supposed to address under-representation of women in the Oireachtas, but there are other aspects that we have to bear in mind.

Women have been under-represented in the Oireachtas because of a patriarchal society and the fact that women have been excluded from decision making for a long time. In order to address this, we need to tackle the underlying problem, which is the lack of women in positions of influence and the fact that women’s perspectives and voices are often excluded.

The quota system should be used as a means of addressing that problem, but it should not be used as a means of achieving a particular political objective by the back door. We have to be careful that we do not replace one problem with another.

The quota system is a tool that can be used to address under-representation, but it is not a solution in and of itself. We need to tackle the underlying problem, which is the lack of women in positions of influence and the fact that women’s perspectives and voices are often excluded.

The importance of the press is often misunderstood or underestimated. Our democracy depends on the ability of journalists to report accurately and fearlessly. They are the eyes and ears of the public, holding the powerful to account and providing a vital source of information. We must never take for granted the role of a free press in a healthy, functioning democracy.

As my hon. Friend the Member for Bexhill and Battle said, there are some 3,000 journalists currently working in Syria, many of them local reporters, often working under extreme conditions. They risk their lives every day in order to report on the conflict and bring news to the rest of the world. Their work is invaluable, and they are doing a vital job in highlighting the suffering of the Syrian people and holding the Syrian regime to account.

Last year, Reporters Without Borders ranked Syria as the most dangerous country in the world for journalists, and it has been that way for the past four years. Between 2011 and 2014, 109 journalists were killed in the line of duty in Syria. That is a staggering number, and it highlights the danger that journalists face every day in Syria.

The Syrian Government’s deliberate targeting of journalists is an outrage, but it is not the only problem. However, it did not provide a legal basis for the exercise of legislative competence by the Welsh Government, nor for the establishment of the devolved competence framework.

The Act set out a list of matters that were reserved to the UK Parliament, with everything else being devolved to the National Assembly for Wales. However, the list of reserved matters was not exhaustive, and the Act also provided for the creation of a Joint Ministerial Committee to consider any devolution issues that were not covered by the reserved matters list.

The Joint Ministerial Committee consisted of the UK Government and the Welsh Government. The Committee's decisions were binding and could not be challenged in the courts.

The Joint Ministerial Committee was replaced by the UK-Wales Joint Ministerial Committee, which was established by the Wales Act 2017. We believe that we can strike this balance by introducing a mechanism for annual rent reviews for existing tenancies that ensures that rents are not increased unreasonably. We propose to achieve this balance by implementing an annual rent review process in rent pressure zones that is fair for tenants and landlords.

Under the proposed rent review mechanism, a landlord will be permitted to increase the rent of an existing tenancy in a rent pressure zone annually by up to 4% of the market rent. However, this annual increase cannot exceed the rate of inflation (as measured by the Consumer Price Index), and the landlord must provide the tenant with a 60 days’ written notice of the proposed increase.

The proposed rent review process is designed to take into account the time elapsed since the last rent setting and any changes in the market rent. It ensures that the rent is increased reasonably over time while protecting tenants from excessive rent increases.

The proposed rent review mechanism is also intended to prevent the incentivisation of annual rent reviews for existing tenancies. 1. Use your phone to its fullest advantage. If you don’t already, download and use apps to assist with things like medication reminders, communication, or therapy activities.

5. Purchase or create sensory boxes or bins. These can be used to help soothe a child and help them self-regulate.
6. Find a support group or network. Having a community of people who understand your child’s challenges can help you feel less isolated and can provide a wealth of helpful ideas and resources.
7. Invest in adaptive equipment if necessary. This can include things like specialized seating, communication devices, or adaptive toys.
8. Create a safe and accessible environment. This may include things like removing trip hazards, installing handrails, or adding childproof latches.

Today, I would like to talk about one of Canada's most decorated soldiers, a true Canadian hero, Warrant Officer Patrice Vincent.

Patrice Vincent was born in St-Jovite, Quebec, in 1963. After graduating from the Canadian Forces Leadership and Recruit School in 1984, Warrant Officer Vincent served as a soldier with the 2nd Battalion, Royal 22nd Regiment, in Valcartier, Quebec. In 1987, he volunteered for the Canadian Airborne Regiment and joined the 1st Battalion, Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, in Edmonton. In 1990, he deployed with the Canadian Airborne Regiment as part of the United Nations peacekeeping mission in Cyprus.

In 1996, he was a member of the Joint Task Force Two and he was part of the team that rescued the crew of Air Algérie Flight AH5017 in the Sahara Desert in 1994. He was also a member of the Joint Task Force Two team that freed Canadian hostage Robert Fowler in 1997.

On December 2, 2009, Warrant Officer Vincent deployed to Afghanistan as a member of the 1st Battalion, Royal 22nd Regiment, serving as a platoon sergeant in the Kandahar provincial reconstruction team. On October 20, 2014, he was killed in a hit-and-run attack while driving his armoured vehicle in Quebec City.

I have never met a survivor of the Holocaust or of any other genocide. I have, however, met survivors of the Armenian Genocide, the Cambodian Genocide, and the Rwandan Genocide, among others. And I can tell you that their stories and the stories of the millions who were lost are all too real, and they are not just numbers in a history book. They are the stories of mothers and fathers, of sons and daughters, of grandparents, siblings, and friends. And to question these stories, to deny that they happened, is to deny the humanity of these people, to deny the humanity of every person who suffered at the hands of a brutal and hateful regime.

And to spread this kind of hatred and ignorance in a classroom, to subject children to this kind of antisemitism and Holocaust denial, is unforgivable. This teacher should be stripped of his license, and he should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.

We cannot allow the memories of the Holocaust and the lessons it teaches to be erased or distorted. We must remember, and we must act to prevent such atrocities from happening again. This teacher’s actions are a direct threat to that mission, and we must hold him accountable for his actions.

We must also take this opportunity to educate ourselves and our communities about the Holocaust and the lessons it teaches. We must remember the six million Jews who were killed, as well as the Roma, the disabled, the LGBTQ+ community, and others who were targeted and exterminated. We must remember the concentration camps and the death marches. We must remember the stories of the survivors, and we must never forget the lessons of the Holocaust.

- Drug Use: Refers to any use of drugs, including legal drugs like alcohol and prescription medications.
- Drug Misuse: Refers to the use of drugs in a way that deviates from the intended use and causes harm to the user.
- Substance Use Disorder: Is a medical condition in which a person experiences impaired control over the use of substances, compulsive use, or continued use despite adverse consequences. The term encompasses a range of disorders, from mild to severe, that can affect any person, regardless of age, gender, race, or ethnicity.
- Addiction: Is a complex, chronic, and relapsing brain disorder that is characterized by compulsive drug seeking and use, despite harmful consequences. It is a medical illness that affects both the brain and behavior.
- Recovery: Is a process of change through which individuals improve their health and wellness, live self-directed lives, and strive to reach their full potential. Recovery is a journey of healing and transformation that can occur in various settings and involves a variety of support services.
- Overdose: Is a medical emergency that occurs when a person takes too much of a substance, such as an opioid, and their body is unable to metabolize it. Overdose can result in respiratory depression, coma, and even death.
- Harm Reduction: Is a set of practical strategies and ideas aimed at reducing negative consequences associated with drug use. Harm reduction approaches focus on improving health outcomes and reducing the risk of drug-related harm, such as overdose, HIV transmission, and hepatitis.

First, we will increase the maximum amount of the Covid Restart Grant to €10,000 for small businesses. This grant will be available to businesses who have suffered a 25% reduction in turnover as a result of the Covid-19 pandemic.

Second, we will extend the period for the Temporary Wage Subsidy Scheme and the Employment Wage Subsidy Scheme for eligible businesses.

The Temporary Wage Subsidy will be extended until 30 April 2021, and the Employment Wage Subsidy Scheme will be extended until 31 December 2021.

The rate of the Temporary Wage Subsidy Scheme will be reduced to 70% for the period from 1 January 2021 to 31 March 2021, and to 50% for the period from 1 April 2021 to 30 April 2021.

The Employment Wage Subsidy Scheme will continue to provide a subsidy of 50% of the weekly remuneration of an eligible employee.

Third, we will introduce a new Restart Fund to provide additional support to businesses that are most impacted by the pandemic.

The Restart Fund will provide grants of up to €40,000 to businesses that have suffered a 50% reduction in turnover as a result of the Covid-19 pandemic.

There is a civil war within Yemen, but the Saudis are not responsible for it. They are there to prevent the Houthis from taking control of Yemen, which would be a major strategic victory for Iran. The Houthis are not a humanitarian problem; they are a strategic problem, a problem for the security of the Gulf region and of the Middle East as a whole. The Saudis are there because they are fighting a war on behalf of the legitimate Government of Yemen.

I am not sure the Deputy is aware of the work done in relation to proxy voting. I would be happy to meet him to discuss the matter further. The question of whether the board can give authority to a credit union director to vote on its behalf in his or her absence is covered in the Credit Union Act 2012 and is dealt with in regulations made by the Minister for Finance. The Act provides that a director may be given authority to vote on behalf of the board in his or her absence. This authority is given to the director in writing and is limited to the period and the matters to which it relates.

The purpose of this provision is to facilitate the efficient running of the board of a credit union by allowing the board to delegate the authority to vote to another director or the chairman of the board in the absence of a director who would otherwise be unable to attend meetings due to work or other commitments.

The Deputy is correct that the current rules on proxy voting are restrictive and do not allow for the delegation of voting rights at a general meeting to another member. In order to allow for such delegation, it is necessary to amend the Credit Union Act 1997, which will require legislation to amend the Act.

The Central Bank of Ireland is currently considering the issue of proxy voting as part of a review of the regulatory framework for credit unions. The current legislation, the Canadian Security Intelligence Service Act, was enacted in 1984. Since that time, there have been some amendments to the legislation. CSIS is allowed to disclose the information to another security agency, but there is no provision for CSIS to disclose personal information to a federal or provincial police agency. There is no provision that allows CSIS to disclose information to an international partner agency, and there is no provision that allows CSIS to disclose information to the public.

The eurozone finance ministers discussed the European Commission's proposal for a eurozone budget on Tuesday, but they did not approve it. They also did not approve the other elements of the Commission's proposal, including the EU-wide tax on digital companies and the reform of the EU's long-term budget.

The finance ministers' meeting was a discussion round, where member states exchanged views and concerns about the Commission's proposal. The ministers did not take any formal decisions, and their conclusions will be presented to the European Council, which will decide on the matter.

President Macron's role in the negotiations is limited to that of any other head of government. He does not have a formal role in the decision-making process. The European Council is the ultimate decision-making body on such matters, and it will make its decision based on the opinions of the finance ministers, the European Commission, and the European Parliament.

In short, while the finance ministers' discussion round was a positive step towards the creation of a eurozone budget, it is not accurate to say that they have effectively approved it, or that President Macron has "won." The European Council will make the final decision.

First, on the statutory register of beneficial ownership. I have made no secret of the fact that I have been a supporter of the principle of a statutory register for many years. I have been working on it with others for many years, and I am delighted that we are now at the stage where we are debating a Bill that contains the provision that we have all been working towards.

However, I am concerned that the provisions in the Bill are not as comprehensive as they need to be, and I would urge the Government to reconsider their approach. The Bill sets out a threshold of control that is far too low for a register of beneficial ownership, and it has been criticised by experts for that reason. In my view, the Government’s approach, which is effectively to establish a register of beneficial ownership based on the legal definition of beneficial ownership in the Companies Act 2006, is too narrow and will not be effective in identifying the true owners of UK companies.

I am afraid that, once again, the Government’s approach seems to be driven by the desire to minimise the number of companies that will be required to disclose their beneficial ownership information, rather than by a desire to establish a register that will be effective in identifying the true owners of UK companies.

The UK’s International Development Committee has now published a report on the UK’s international response to the pandemic. Its recommendations include:

- DFID should use its resources to support low-income countries to respond to the pandemic, as well as to support a global recovery
- The UK should support multilateral organisations, including the World Health Organisation (WHO), to provide leadership in the global response
- The UK should do more to support the poorest people and most vulnerable communities, including in conflict and fragile states

I agree with these recommendations. I also think that we should do more to support the poorest and most vulnerable communities in the UK, including by strengthening our international development system to be better able to respond to crises such as the pandemic.

## DFID’s work on the pandemic

As the UK’s development agency, DFID is using its resources to support low-income countries to respond to the pandemic, and to support a global recovery. This includes:

- Providing funding to the WHO, the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) and the World Food Programme to support their work on the pandemic
- Providing funding to the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement to support their humanitarian response to the pandemic, including in conflict and fragile states
- Providing funding to UNICEF and the World Bank to support a global response to the pandemic

she is released, but the term of imprisonment is not legally spent. The period of parole is a period of supervision. It is not a period of time spent in the community.

The supervision continues until the parole order is revoked. When the parole order is revoked, the person goes back to prison. In this case, the person is not considered to have been at liberty. The time in the community spent while on parole is not credited as time served in prison. That is a fundamental point. It is not a matter of the person spending time in custody, or not, it is a matter of the parole order being revoked and the period of supervision coming to an end.

The order must provide for a specified time. The period of supervision may be up to three years, but it may be less if the Board of Parole considers that to be appropriate. The period of parole is a period of supervision, not a period of time in the community spent by the person on parole.

This has led to the hoarding of vaccines by some countries while others have no access to vaccines.

The Government amendments are aimed at ensuring that the benefits of the Bill are directed only to those in need and to ensure that the system is not open to abuse.

The Government amendments are also designed to ensure that there is some consistency in the benefits system. At present, people on income support receive the same amount whether they are living in a one-bedroomed flat in London or a four-bedroomed house in the north of Scotland. The amendments will ensure that, as the cost of living varies from region to region, the level of housing benefit will also vary.

The Government amendments do not prevent the use of local housing allowance but they do not encourage it, either. Under the provisions of the Bill, local housing allowance would be available to certain people who are living in accommodation that is not part of a private rented sector tenancy. The Government amendments will ensure that local housing allowance is not available to people who have entered into a private rented sector tenancy, because the benefit system should be fair to all taxpayers.

Local housing allowance was a complex idea when it was first floated, and the Government did not support it. However, the provisions of the Bill and the Government amendments will ensure that there is a safety net for people who find themselves homeless or in a temporary situation.

It was a difficult time for Labour. The miners’ strike had been lost, the poll tax had been brought in, and the Tories were riding high.

The feeling that there was no alternative to the Tories was pervasive in those days. I remember going to my local Labour club and hearing the constant refrain that “Labour would never win an election again.”

The election of 1992 had been a disaster. Labour had been trounced. The Tories had won their fourth consecutive election and they were on a roll.

But the death of John Smith changed everything.

The Labour leadership had never been more united or more united around a common purpose. It was an incredible moment and it was a moment that I will never forget.

I remember watching the news and seeing the crowd gather outside John Smith’s house in Fulham. I remember the tears in the eyes of his friends and family.

I remember the moment when Tony Blair took to the stage and said, “We have lost a great leader but we have not lost hope.”

I remember the moment when the Labour Party elected a new leader and it was Tony Blair.

I remember the moment when the Tories were finally defeated and Labour won the election.

I remember the moment when Tony Blair stood in Downing Street and said, “We have a mandate to change Britain.”

I remember the moment when the Labour Party was reborn and the Tories were vanquished.

I remember the moment when Tony Blair stood in the House of Commons and said, “We are a government of the many, not the few.”

I remember the moment when Tony Blair stood in the European Union and said, “We are a member of the European Union but we will never surrender our sovereignty.”

The review was conducted by the independent reviewer of firefighters’ pensions, the Rt Hon Lord Hutton of Furness. I would like to place on record my thanks to Lord Hutton and his team for their hard work and dedication.

The review was carried out to address concerns about the affordability and sustainability of the firefighters’ pension scheme, and to ensure that it remains fair and attractive to current and future firefighters. The Government have accepted the vast majority of Lord Hutton’s recommendations.

The review confirmed that the scheme is affordable and sustainable, but that it would be prudent to make changes to ensure that this remains the case. I would like to stress that the changes we are making to the pension scheme are designed to ensure that the scheme remains attractive and fair to current and future firefighters.

We will be taking steps to improve the flexibility of the scheme by introducing a career average revalued earnings pension scheme, or CARE scheme, for firefighters. This will provide a more secure and attractive pension for future firefighters, while also ensuring that the scheme remains affordable.

We will also be addressing the issue of the firefighters’ age discrimination claims. The review found that the current pension age is unfair and discriminatory, as it is higher than the State pension age for women. The Government have agreed to reduce the pension age for women to 60, in line with the State pension age, and to bring forward the pension age for men to 60 over a shorter period than under the current scheme. I have always been clear that I cannot support a deal that involves a hard border in Northern Ireland, or indeed a customs border with the European Union. The withdrawal agreement that the Prime Minister negotiated and the subsequent political declaration do not meet that test. I have been working hard to seek a solution and I have been in discussions with colleagues in recent days and nights. I understand the concerns that have been raised about the Irish backstop and the risk that it could indefinitely trap the UK in a customs union with the European Union. I agree that the backstop is a problem, but I do not believe that there is a solution to this problem which can be found within the existing withdrawal agreement.

I have been very clear with the Prime Minister that I cannot support a deal that includes the backstop, and I have been talking to him about my concerns about the backstop and about the need for a legally binding unilateral exit mechanism from the backstop. I believe that the Prime Minister shares those concerns and is open to finding a solution to this problem.

We need to be realistic about the options available to us and the time that remains. It is important to remember that the backstop is an insurance policy. It is not the default position; it is an insurance policy that the parties agreed would kick in if they could not agree any other solution.

That is why, having considered all the options, I believe that the best way forward is to seek a legally binding unilateral exit mechanism that would remove the need for the backstop altogether. I understand that the European Union has said that it will not renegotiate the withdrawal agreement, but I do not believe that we should abandon our efforts to seek a solution to this problem.

I am pleased that the Government are starting to take my calls seriously, as they have recently pledged to consult on a national suicide prevention strategy. That is a huge step forward, but it is not enough. We need a strategy, and we need one now.

The strategy must include a wide range of measures to prevent suicide. We know that many of the risk factors for suicide are linked to mental health problems, so it is crucial that we provide mental health services that are accessible and tailored to meet the needs of men. We must also address the stigma surrounding mental health, because that prevents men from seeking help when they need it.

I am a strong supporter of the mental health five-year forward view, and I welcome the Government’s commitment to parity of esteem between physical and mental health. I also believe that we need to take a public health approach to suicide prevention, and that means tackling the root causes of suicide. We must address issues such as alcohol misuse, homelessness, domestic violence and unemployment, all of which are linked to an increased risk of suicide.

The government is not planning to sell these sites but to give them away to developers in return for housing.

St. Michael's Estate is a 33-acre site in the north inner city, between the North Strand and the Dublin Port, and is one of the largest State-owned sites in Dublin City. It is also one of the most important sites for urban regeneration in the city. This site has been under the control of the State for almost a century. It was taken into public ownership during the 1920s.

The plan is to give it away to a developer in return for 1,450 housing units, half of which are to be affordable units. The developer will then have the right to develop the site over a 20-year period.

The State has failed to build adequate social housing for the last number of decades, and the result has been the current crisis. Yet, now, the Government is proposing to give away prime sites to developers without any obligation to ensure that they build the social housing which is needed. This is not good enough.

Labour has a different plan. We propose to rezone the entire St. Michael's Estate as a strategic development zone. This would allow for the rapid development of housing, commercial space, retail space, and other facilities to be provided on the site, in line with local needs. We would also require the developer to build 100% affordable units on the site, with a mix of social and affordable housing.

The current plan is a missed opportunity for the north inner city, for housing, and for Dublin. We should be seizing this opportunity to develop St. Michael's as a model for urban regeneration in the city, and to provide the housing and the jobs which the area needs.

This G7 investment was announced at the "Women's Empowerment and G7 Leaders' Summit," held on June 7 and 8, 2018, in Charlevoix, Quebec. The summit was attended by leaders from G7 countries, as well as representatives from global organizations and civil society groups.

Canada's goal for the summit was to establish new partnerships to increase women's access to quality education, especially for those living in the poorest countries. The G7 leaders also committed to improving the collection of gender-disaggregated data to better understand the challenges that girls and women face in accessing education.

The G7 leaders emphasized that education is key to advancing gender equality and improving health, nutrition and economic outcomes for women and girls. They agreed to work towards the goal of ensuring that all girls and women complete their primary education by 2030, as part of the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals.

In addition to the education investment, the G7 leaders also committed to taking action to eliminate gender-based violence, promote women's entrepreneurship, and increase the number of women in leadership positions.

Overall, the Women's Empowerment and G7 Leaders' Summit was an important step forward in the global effort to promote gender equality and empower women and girls. The G7's commitment to investing in education and taking action to eliminate gender-based violence and promote women's empowerment sends a strong message that gender equality is a priority for these countries. It is also an important reminder that gender equality is essential for achieving sustainable development and improving the lives of people around the world.

It is crucial that we continue to keep the pressure on the insurance industry and the Government to ensure that we can reduce the cost of insurance.

Many of the businesses I represent have been affected by the cost of insurance. They are very concerned about the impact it has on their businesses and their ability to operate. The cost of insurance is causing a significant impact on our economy, particularly in rural Ireland. It is also causing difficulty for clubs and societies, including GAA clubs. I was reading a report on the cost of insurance for GAA clubs. It is estimated that the cost of insurance for a GAA club has increased by 2,300% in 15 years, which is absolutely astronomical. There is a real concern that clubs may struggle to continue operating in these circumstances.

The cost of insurance is having a significant impact on many businesses, including farmers. A number of farmers have told me that they are struggling to get insurance and that the cost is prohibitive. Many have had to cancel their policies or, worse, have had their claims rejected. This is having a significant impact on their ability to operate and is adding to the difficulties they are already facing in rural Ireland.

The Prime Minister is cutting the jobs of 14,000 construction workers, cancelling the Green Jobs programme, scrapping the Regional Development Agencies and abolishing the Sustainable Development Commission.

All these decisions will cost us jobs and will slow the rate of recovery. They are the worst possible decisions at the worst possible time.

We need a plan for growth. I am working with the Labour Business Commission and business leaders across the country to put together a credible plan for recovery and growth that is rooted in the needs of business.

We need to create a million new green jobs. We need to increase our investment in infrastructure and renewable energy. We need to support our manufacturing industries and rebuild our transport links.

A plan for growth must include a plan for business. We need to reform our tax system so that it is fair, simple and encourages business investment. We need to reform our banking system so that it serves the needs of small businesses.

The Prime Minister has no plan for growth and no plan for business. He is making reckless and damaging decisions which will cost jobs and slow the recovery.

We need a plan for growth which is focused on job creation and backed by the business community. We need a plan which will give Britain the confidence to rebuild and recover.

I am working on that plan, and when we are in government we will deliver it.
